Terttig. THE ELATE-BOTTLE FLY. Buzzing and gay in the early dawn, Fresh from a nap on the parlour wall, Out for a flight over garden and lawn, Fearing no tumble and dreading no fall, Came a fly: A lively, frolicsome, blue-bottle fly; And his feet Were as neat, And his style As complete, AS his brain Was replete with the mischief that laughed in his eye I o, What glorious fun I'll have to-day, When the baby's asleep and the nurse away; When Rover lies by the kitchen door; I'll waken them both and make them roar! Oh, what larks !" Cried the rollicking, reckless, blue-bottle "What a cry," Bald the fly, "There will be After me, When I've done With my fun!" And he wickedly winked his wee eye! " Then I'll go and dance on grandpa's head, While he struggles to,prush me away; And tickle his ear till he'll wish I was dead And over the table at dinner I'll play Back and forth. And feast on thecrumba from a freshly -baked pie! And I'll sip From the lip Of each glass That may pass All sweet things Dinner brings !" Quoth this riotous blue-bottle fly. But, alas for the plans he had laid! And alas for the day just begun ! For this fly soon lit in the to ateful shade To escape the ho'' rays of the sun; And to dream Of the sights that 3henhl 00011 gfcet his eye; When unseen, ' From the greeu Of a limb Above Limn, On his head, By a thread, Fell a spider, Who coolly devoured that blue-bottle fly. —Leeds Weekly Mercury.

How TO BE HEAT:rim—Eat very slowly, with a view to the thorough 'mastication of your food; rather forego a meal, oc take but half the needful quentity, than eat too fast.—ltefrain from both mental and bodily exertion for a short time after the principal meal. If immediate exer-ni tion he required, only a slight repast should be taken, in.' steal of the usual meal. Never eat a fall meal when the hcsae is much ',heated or mach fatigued with exer- cise. WM* 'ntil you are somewhat refreshed by a short interval of :wee. Occasional abstinence. Whenever I the system is teaele or disordered, diminish the quantity of your food and allow yourself more time for exercise. In ' cases of slight indisposition, a partial or a total fast will often be found the best restorative.—Take no physic un- less it be absolutely necessary. Learn, if possible, how to keep well without it. In case of rePl indisposition, consult a me lical adviser without' delay, and implicitly attend to , his directions so far as you think he is fully acquainted with your constitution and with the best means of treating your disorder. Never risk your health and life, either by I neglecting serious illness or by tampering with quack reme- dies.--Gentle exercise should be taken regularly two hours a day at least; and it must never be forgotten that c.heerfuln&as is an essential ingredient in all beneficial exer- cise. Mental relaxation in agreeable society, too, should be soughs as often as due attention to business and other imottant affairs will permit. Liveee larennet.:--While waiting for a jury, Judge Cary, of Arkansas, after listening to some tough dog stories, said :—" These are curious yarns, gentlemen, but I be- lieve them all. I had a dog once, back in Nebraska, that I kept to in Illumber." "Beg pardon, judge, but did you Bay the dog herded lumber ?" " Yes, sir—cottonwood boards. We always kept a dog there to bring the lumber in, at night." Everybody now paid the closest attention ,as they knew that the boss was at work. "It was this way:: cotton vood boards warp like thunder in the sun. A board would begin to hump its back up about nine in the morning, and in half an hour it would turn over. By eleven it would warp the other way with the heat, and make another flop. Each time it turned it moved a couple of feet, always following the sun towards the west. The tirst summer I lived in Brownville over ten thousand feet of lumber skipped out to the hills the day before I advertised house raisin'. I went to the country to attend a lawsuit, and when I got back there wasn't a stick of timber left. It strayed away into the uplands. An ordinary board would limb a two-mile hill during a 114 t week, and when it struck the timber it would keep wet /Au' in and out among the , trees like a garter snake. Every farmer in the State had to keep shepherd dogs to follow his lumber around the coun- try, hold it together, and sbow where it wasain the morn- ing. We didn't need any flumes there for lumber. We sawed it east of the place where we wanted to use it, and let it warp itself to its destination; with men and doff,. • - it off at the right time, we never lost a stiel- arr?" hen continued the judge. The witeres lied, to I guess they disagreed !".—Litt',, Rock Gazette. Tau CONTENTED NIOCIEE.—" A leetle money will bey wood an' tatere an' bacon an shoes an' cloze," began the old man, as the meetiat!, Opened. "Lots of money will bay silks an' satins an 'jewelry an' white houses. De man vrid a leetle money tems to believe at de man wid lots of it am takin' all de comfort. I used to have dat idea, but Ire got ober it. It am my solumn belief dat de man who eote down befo' his own lire, wid his wife on de right, and his chill'en on de left, an' de ole cat an' a panful o' apples in de middle, am in position to take jist as much comfort as if be lived in a house avid golden sta'rs. Take de world frew an you'll fin' dat de humblest home am de happiest. De man who has steady work, a savia' wife an healthy chill'en, wouldn't be a bit happier if he was to draw $50,000 in a lottery. It he don't take comfort it's his own fault. It's her own fault if his wife isn't happy. Sometimes my ole woman gitsthe blues an' blows aroun' kase she sees odder folks ride out in der keeridges an' dress up in der satans, but I build up a good fire, git out de apples, cider an' pop-corn, draw up de big ruckin-cheer, and the can't stand it ober ten minits. De bluos begin to fly away, and she pat de bald spot on my head an' sa3.s We has a cabin of our own, plenty to eat, a little money in the bank, and I 'spect we kin sot down an' take as much solid comfort as if you war guv'ner and I had ten silk dresses.' He who makes de most of what he's got am fitting hisself to enjoy it better. No situation but what could be made worse. Ebery dollar made by honest work ought to brihg two dollars' werf of so id comfort. Wid dese few remarks, called forth by over- hearin' groutlin' aroun' bekase be couldn't have mashetrtiters at ebery meel, we will now eradicate to de usual order of bueinise:" `` '

div.head: LAND QUEST ON,
div.p: THE LAND QUEST ON,

- VIII. Dating almost the whole of last Session the British Parlia- ment devoted its energies to the passing of an Act for thebene- fit of the Irish farmers, whose legitimate grievances had long been admitted by. all well-informed persons, and as to the necessity of remedying which, even a mijority of the Es- tate Agents who gave evidence before the Bessborough Commission, agreed. The Irish Tenant Farmer now pos- sesses the benefit or protection of an Act which gives him by law pretty much what some of the best of landowners had already given their tenants voluntarily, and every well wisher of Ireland will unite in the desire that the operation of the new Land Act will result in a reign of peace and prosperity in that hitherto unfortunate country. It is too much to ask or expect that as the British Parlia- ment:devoted the whole of last Session to the cause of the Irish farmer, that at least some per Con of next Session sla ill be occupied in legislation for the benefit and protec- tion of the English and Scotch farmers. This depends very much on the attitude of the farmers themselves, for 6. who would be free themeelvos must strike tips blow." There is little doubt that the Scottish farmers have sum- . .

cient determination of purpose and control over their repre- sentatives in Parliament, to insist upon their grievances being attended to. They form within a fraction one hal/ the county electors, and of course hold the county seats in their own hands, and they insist on their Parliamentary Candidates pledging themselves to support such legislation as is required. On the other hand, in England, as a whole, the farmers only constitute about one fourth of the entire body of county electors. In the strictly agricultural di- visions they axe, however, much stronger, and carry with them a very large body of village tradesmen and artisans, who are dependent on their custom or are willing to look to them for advice. They therefore hold the balance ot power in their hands, and could. if they thought fit, exclude any candidate who declined to 'pledge himself to their views, or on the other hand compel the county landlords, for the sake of their votes, to surrender the second seats to Tenant Farmer representatives. But it is too generally the case that the English farmers put " confidence ' in political candidates who look on the farmers as persons in the land- ' lord's service, to be kept in good humour if possible, but to receive nothing either of substantial power or redress of grievances, so long as fair words will do. Of course if the farmers like that sort of thing, there is an end of it, but they certainly do seem to put up with what people in large I towns would not stand. I It is all very well for prejudiced people to charge those w'io wish to reform our present system with desiriog to' net 1 class against class, and the tenant against his landlord. There is no foundation whatever for such a charge. We I repudiate Parnell and all his works. Our motto is "Live and let live." We are glad to 'be able to say there are se.ores of landlords in this country of whom England may be proud —that the landlords have their rights as well as the tenants, lint the landlords have also duties which they do not al ways perform, while the tenant's righta are not yet legalised. There are many places in England where, owing to our present system of tenants holding subject to only six mouths' notice to quit, without any leg.a/ claim to be paid for any improvements they have made in their holding, however much they may have cost, and which the landlord has the legal right to " confiscate" (a favourite word with our Tory friends) and often does,—those are the districtt where, as the saying goes, the tenant farmer "belongs to his landlord body, soul, and breeches," and where the toe- veiling motto is " FearUpd, hoßoar the King, and knuckle down to your Landlord." . Let ns, however, take a brief glance at the depressed state of British agriculture, which demands the introduction of some changes in the law and the system, for the benefit of landlord and tenant alike, and also in the general interests of the whole community. English and ,Scottish farmers have suffered as much, if not more, than Irish tenants for a numbe- of -years past, bat not being so in the habit 'of living from hand to mouth as the small farmers in Ireland, the distress has not been so acute, and they have been bravely and patiently waiting for oetter seasons, gradually eating into their reserve capital meanwhile, until thousands of them have been ruined. Mr. Caird, in a speech not very long ago, showed that the returns of the Iri,h farmers during the last ten years have been much more favourable than those of the sister countries. They have rapidly di- minished their dependence on wheat, the acreage of which has decreased more than one-third. They have been placing their reliance more on the rearing of cattle, and the produce of the dairy, for both of which the prices have been good: The small farms, requiring litt e expenditure Sf hired labour, have enabled them to escape the growing labour bills of the large farms of this country. For similar reasons the West of England and most parte of Scotland have not suf- fered with anything like the severity of the more purely corirdistricta of England, whose dependence is chiefly on wheat, and where the system of large farms is necesearily accompanied by increased labour bills. In seven out of ten I years the seasons have been wet and chilly, and this has I pressed with special severity on the crops which thrive best with abundance of heat and sunlight. There are few I parishes from the Humber to the Solent in which farms I have not been surrendered to their owners, and some in which farms are absolutely tenantless The local bankers, \ for their own protection, have been compelled to withhold credit, and tenants wish diminished capital and restricted ~"'islit 1100 kpund' it neeevaary to retire fr9m larg holdtog!, arid either take strialler farrnk or quit the busineo. In every county one meets with insticces of considerable es- tates with six or eight farms thrown cn the landlord's hands, and certain localities can be named ,where, within,a 1 mile or two of thriving towns; thine are hundreds of acres of clay land entirely deserted, and on which there has ,ppt I been a furrow turned for two years. It is in 'such circum- stances no longer a question of redection of rent or of ontlay ' on improvements. The tenants have left, the neighbonr- hood, employment of labour has ceased, and 'the landlords and their agents, even if they had the means,can have little hope of gaining a profit where a hardworking farmer • has failed. The entire area of corn in Ireland is not more than half of that of the eleven principal corn counties of Eng- land upon which this heavy loss has fallen, and if measured in money the loss of capital in Ireland occasioned by the seasons would bear no comparison with. that of England. So much for Mr. Caird. The importatian in recent years of immense quantities of American wheat at low prices, one would have thought, would have irduced our farmers to have turned their atte 1- tion more to stockraising and dairying; but here again We.., have a sad evidence of the extent of agricultural depression for the amount of live stock is a sure guide to the tivanclaii position of tenant, farmers. The following figures (which, recently appeared in The Times) speak for themselves, showing that there are now £19,000,000 worth of animals , less in the Vuited; Kingdom than there were seven years ago :
Decrease of Lice Stcck in the United Kingdom. Cattle. Sheep. Pigs. No. in 1874. ... 10,281,036 34,837,597 3,337,354 „ 1881. 9,904,033 ... 27,899,937 3,149,875
*reckoning cattle at £l2, sheep at £2, and pigs at £1 10s. per head.

It may be argued that the above disastrous results are occasioned by unfavourable seasons, which cannot be helped.; ' But admitting that that I-. se rolta great extent, is there not all the more reason to 'rembire the other hin- drances of the farmer which ctr.l be helped? Bad laws have helped bad seasons, and made them worse. If reforms in our present system will tend to induce capital once mere to flow into these thousands of uncultivated or semi-culti- vated acres, will it not benefit the la.ndletd ao w,il a the tenant ? Certainly it will. But to resume our review. Tbe very magnitude of the ! agricultural question should claim fur it the early I attention of rarliamebt. It is estimated that. '.1,6 people im.tediately IA in farming humber one-iota of the population—as follows : Landlords, big and little, 8000300; occupie-s :arms, 1,000,000 ; farm labourers, 1,500,000; making ;4300,000 persons engaged in the culti- vation and ovrr.:.oBfilp of land, and reckoning their fanflies at two 1D.14-tviduals for every plan directly engaged, we , "ay.r. tetal of si millions of people, who can be considered tho agricultural classes, or ahout oce-fourtb of the inhabit- ants of the United Kingdom. Again, in the Journal of the Royal Agi icultural Society, three years ago, Major Craigie estimated the gross annual in- come of the agricultural classes at about one-seventh that of the entire nation, and as made up as follows Income of Landlords £62,000,000 Income of Tithe Owners 5,000,000 Income of Farmers Earnings of Labourers

Total £158,000,000 Now to the same extent as that income is increased or diminished, so will the general welfare and prosperity of the rest of the community be affected. If by just and well- considered reforms in our present system, capital can be at- tracted to the development of the resources of the soil and its consequent increased productiveness, every £1,000,000 of additional wealth will tend to- improve and revive the home trade, and wines certainly benefit all other classes of the nation. It is evident, then, that it is of the highest im- portance to every individual trade and business that the in- come of the agricultural classes should be increased, and their prosperity restored and permanently established. An estimate has been recently made by combining the detailed valuations of Mr. Caird, Mr. James Howard, M.P., Mr. John Algernon Clarke, and other agricultural statisticians, as published in the Journal of the Royal Agricultural Society, and elsewhere, and the result arrived at is that in 1880 the average yearly value of the salable produce of our fields and farmsteads, in corn, hay, straw, roots, vegetables, frets, and .special crops, and in meat, wool, dairy produce, other animal products, horses, and poultry—approached £300,000,000, or about £8 108. per head of the population. Now it is contended by those who understand the neces- sities of modern farming that the conditions under which the cultivation of the soil is carried on in Great Britain are highly detrimental to agricultural prosperity, being opposed to increased production, and therefore prejudicial to the in- terests not only of the landlords and tenants, but also of the whole community, and that if those obnoxious con- ditions were removed, the produce of the soil could be easily increased 50 per cent, at least, and instead of pro- ducing £500,000,000 out of the soil, that sum might be in- creased to £450,000,000, or another £150,000,000 towards the home trade of this country. Lord Derby in known as possessing a calm and judicial mind, and his utterances am 3 blivariably weighty and reliable. Yet he said not many years ago—" We do not get as yet out of English earth one half of what we probably might with advantage, if all our

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, NOVEMPER 19, 1881

present resources Xere brought to bear upon the soil." i Other similar evidence might be quoted showing that the paramount object of future reforms should be " INCREASED PRODUCTION, ' and this, combined with "DECREASED COST" in the form of reduced rents, tithe., taxes, and rail- way charges (to be dealt with in subsequent articles), will enable the British farmer to hold his own against all comers. Our present system has broken down, and agri- culture as a business is no longer remunerative. The cir- cumstances of the case will compel early Parliamentary at- tention. The hour has arrived, and so have the men, for an association of agricultural reformers has coins into exis- tence, known as "The Farmer's Alliance," worthy of the support of every farmer in the country.

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE -CULTURE, ea. 7 ENRICHING Onceranns.—Any farmer who has been accustomed to raising apples, and has been uniformly enc. ceseful, will doubtless say that if he expects to get good crops he treats the orchard as he does for any other crop. He manures" it, and he finds that a manure that will do for most other crops will do for the crop of apples. It is the neglect to manure orchards at all, that causes them to be so poorly and the trees to look in bad condition; nothing is better than wood ashes for orchards, if we had the ashes; but nearly everybody burns coal, except in certain out-of- the-way sections, and we must, therefore, resort to some- thing else. Next to wood ashes there is no fertiliser better that§ barnyard manure. A liberal application of this, if only once in three years, with careful pruning and scraping of the trees, and ferretting out the borers and all other in- sects which lay concealed under the bark, will soon make a change in the productiveness of the orchard. October and November are the best months to apply the manure and to gisre the trunks of- the trees a good scraping off 0 old' bark. If the tennis were washed with whale oil soap, say lib. to a bucket of water; there 'would not be many insects alive after the operation.—Nebraska Farmer. PREJUDICE OF GARDENERS AGAINST BEES.—It is a re- markable fact that although gardeners as a rule are intel- ligent and fairly educated men, they have crotcheta which are almost irradicable. Many entertain a mistaken notion that bees are mischievous insects,but there are many others who cultivate them—for example, Mr. Ingram, of Bel voir Castle, who is celebrated for his fine collection of early spring floVsrl, which he-cultivatea chiefly for the use of his bees. This gentleman some two years ago gave an ad- mirable lecture on "Bee Flora" to the British Beekeepers' Association, wherein he proved that the honey-bee was the gardener's best friend. A correspondent of the Norfolk Chronicle states that on a lady in Surrey' stating her 'in- tention of buying soma beasts) her gardener, he immediately gave her notice to leave.' Sir 'John Lubbock, in a lecture recently given at York, observed that "we all know what an acute sense of smell bees have," and then proved their appreciation of colour. Bees have for centuries past been- the Means of improving our fruit and flowers by their fertilising ,power and unwearied indastry. A good era is commencing' for bees; as the prejudice is removed they will be estimated at their true value. TEE SALE OF FARM PRODUCE.—W. F. R. writes to the Chamber of Agriculture Journal :—There is one subject con- nected with.the extreme depression in agricultural matters existing a ihe present time that I should like to bring be- fore the public notice with a hope that a remedy may be found. It is the bad organisation of trade in farming pro- dude now existing. I will give some instances of what I mean. Last May I was in a county town in a central county on market day. I found the price of butter was 18.1 d. to ls. 2d. a lb. 'oCon - the following day I was in the principal .county town also on market day. The price obtained for butter was from le. 4cl. to Is. ed. a pound, and some had sold still higher. A railway runs between the two towns, which are fourteen miles distant from each other. Many farmers take their produce by road twelve miles from the former dietrict to a neighbouring town on account of the bad market at their own, thereby incurring a considerable waste of thatramd locomotion: . A farmeraxplained to me a fortnight.atot he had sold his bullocks at less price than he 'was offered for them last May; he sold them to the local dealers who attend his nearest town, not liking to incur the loss of time that 'Would be caused if he took them to a better market at a distance. These very animals were sold at a large fair which took place a few days after in the same county at many pounds a head profit. One of the largest dealers in cheese, butter, and eggs in the West-end of Lon- don told me that he procured all these articles from abroad —Sweden, America, .Lombardy, or Normandy—and that they were delivered at his establishment with greater regu- larity and of nic;re unvarisible, quality than he could ensure if the-v were obtained from farmers in our country. These three instances will Illustrate my case, but I could bring many more to bear upon it. The producer in the United Kingdom wants such an organieatieri of trade as will enable him to part with the produce on his farm or at the next market readily, and in the assurance .tut he will get the best market price with the least waste of time and energy in obtaining a sale.

The man, Snell, who is charged with the murder of his master in Nottinghamshire; was on Tuesday committed for trial.

Mr. Nicholson, silk manufacturer, is about to provide a free library and museum for Leak. The steamer Alverton, of Cardiff, while on a voyage from Bilbao to Cette, with pig iron, has been totally lost. Crew saved. . _ _
A verdict of manslaughter has, by a coroner's jury, been retuned against a boy named Joiner, at Birmingham, in connection with the death of a girl shot by him on the
sth." The writ for the election of a member of Parliament for Stafford was received on Thursday by the Mayor of the borough, and the election was fixed to take place on Satur-

day. • A person named Watson, Of Openshaw, is in custody, being remanded, for tampering with post-office servants at Manchester, with a view to obtaining information from racing telegrams. Tee sum of £B,OOO bequeathed .by the late Mr. James CLirk, of Ralston, senior partner of Mess-s. Clark and Co., Anchor Mills, Paisley has just been paid over to the treasurer or he Paisley Infirmary. The terms of the concession made by Sir Thomas Glad- stone to his tenantry are that he has given a deduction of 20 per cent. for crop 1881, and has promised 10 per cent. for crop 1882 whether it be favourable or unfavourable. In a cargo of bones from Turkey now being landed at Dundee. a Russian gun cartridge, loaded, was discovered. 'if this cartridge had gone through the machine it might have destroyed the works and the lives of the men employed in them. ,

Addressing an agricultural meeting at Slough, on Satur- day night, Colonel F. Burnaby said that "the Free Trade swindle was devised for the benefit of the rich man, who drew money from foreign securities, and not for ,the tillers of the soil."

On Wednesday morning last the vault of a new church being built at Milan gave way. One workman was killed on the spot, four were picked up in a dyiug state, and two others seriously injured. The disaster is attributed to the bad materials and imperfect construction.

A religious census of Ipswich, taken on Sunday by the East Anglian Daily Times, shows the number who attended places of worship in the morning to be 14,492, out of a popu- lation of 53,000. The Church of England had 6,60 A atten- dants, and the Nonconformists 7,264, while 584 at public institutions where the church service is used.

The strike in the Potteries for an advance of wages is I rapidly extending. It is computed that up to Friday even- ing more than 30,000 operatives were idle—either volun- tarily or by reason of the action of the malcontents,—and on Saturday many additional factories were brought to a stop- page. There is no sign of concession on either side. The Marquis of Lorne' replying to an address presented to the Princess Louise and himself, on Tuesday, by a deputa- tion from the Chester Town Council, expressed himself highly confident in tile loyalty of the Canadians to the mother country. Ile said that England might occasionally he spoken of in Canada as if she were "the old woman who had so many children see did nor know what to do ;' but such language'was probably only used by one person in ten thousand

The summons was granted. •

CHAMBERLAIN ON THE HOURS OF LABOUR.—Mr. Chamberlain, M.P., replying to a letter from the Birmingham Hatters' Assistants' Early Closing, Association, says that Parliament has always declined to interfere with the powers of employment for adult labour, and it would be beyond his jurisdiction to issee recommendations on the, subject in. his official capacity. At the same time, Mr. Chamberlain says he feels great sympathy with the endeavours to reduce ab- normally long days of work, and believes that excessive hours of labour are hurtful to all concerned+ • ,T ANOTHER SUSPECTED OUTRAGE ON THE Ranwly.—The body of a young man, bearing marks of violence, was dis- covered on Tuesday on the line of the Midland Railway, at Beeston, and there is reason to believe that he harr been the victim of foul play. The body was removed to the White Hart Inn, where it has been identified as that ot a young man named Bennett, in the employ of one of the largest lace manufacturers at Nottingham. Very few facts at present have been elicited, but the police are investigating the affair, which is at present surrounded with mystery. A SPrnmes WEB.—Look closely at a net of the diadem garden spider you will recognise the creature by the gem- like whitish markings on the body, and the dark bands and spines on the legs. Those threads which form the spirals are more glutinous than the fine but stronger lines radiating from the centre, where the diadem takes his sentinel-post. Take a magnifying glass, and a multitude of fine globules may be traced along the spiral threads. These constitute a series cf fastenings by which the circular lines are 1 gummed firmly to the radiating threadt.. The number of ' these globules, or web.ties, is surprising, a single net of the , "diadem" spidek having been found to' contain above 1 87,000. ' The net of the Epeira apoclisa, a species allied to the garden diadem spider, usually consists of twenty-six radiating lines, and twenty-four rows of spirals. A large web of this kind has been- calculated to contain 120,000 viscid globules. Beside& the radiating and spiral threads, the observer will not fail to notice the main lines, which extend beyond the geometrical work; and support the whole. These main threads are faatened at each end to leaves Or twigs, and the radiating tines are then firmly se- cured to these supports. If one of these important lines be suddenly broken, the geometrical structure will collapse and become a ruin. Thyw hole of such a net, with all its elabo- rate tracery of radiating and parallel lines, with its thousands upon thousands of points, is sometimes pro- ductd in about forty minutes. A web over a cannon's mouth, or , across the opening in the poor-box, ,is is therefore n ) prcof that either has been long disused. The cannon may have been discharged yesterday, and yet a perfect web be over its mouth' this, morning. The reader will not forget thtt in this short. time the spider not only arranges the fine geometrical lines, Nut also spins the whole from its on tt b,dy. Let the reader examine carefully one I of the fine threads, and then estimate it diameter. Does it not seem almost impossible to express in the fraction of lan inch the thickness of that filmy tissue? But the fine ' line is not a single one, being composed of no less than 4,000 threads. Some of these wonderfully complex lines are themselves so fine that 4,000,000 twisted together would not exceed the thickness 'pf an ordinary hair from the human head. Yet each one of these 4,000,000 tissues 111 Itself composed of 4,000 single threads. The diameter, therefore, of one single thread is but one sixteen thousand- millionth part of the thickness of a human hair. If such a statement seems almost incredible, it is but one of the many mysteries abounding in the lower forms of life.— Cassell's Popular Educator. How zaz Swan' GazW.--As Kitty Coleman and Maggie ' Weirwere going to school one morning, Kitty said," I was over at Uncle Fred's last .Satunlay, and came near staying too late., We had such fun,lhat I did not notice how near the sun was to setting, and I was very much afraid I might meet a tramp." "Did you meet one ?" inquired Maggie. "No one but Johnnie Gates ;.he was coming down the hill whistling, and with a great big water melon under his arm; I was scared at first, but when I saw who it was I got over It," At receas, Marie said to M",;:y Ford, "Kittle told me that bite taw Johnnie Gates carrying a great big water melon home Saturday evening. Wonder where he got it and what he is going to do with it." Before school Mary whispered to Sallie Bates, "Johnnie Gates was seen carry. jug a great big water melon Saturday evening. I wonder if he got it honestly." "Mr. Hart's melon patch was robbed about that time; maybe that's where it came from," answered Sallie. At noon Sallie told Susan and Jennie, "I know something, and I'll tell you if you won't breathe it to a sold." "0 no, we won't," cried both girls in one breath, " what is it ?" "Why, Johnnie Gates robbed Mr. Hart's melon patch one night last week." " 0 dear, isn't that awful I" exclaimed Susie. "I always thought Johnnie was not so much better than the rest of us, for all he made be- lieve he was so honest," said Jennie. "He couldn't have done it alone," Sallie said. Whereupon Jennie hastened to a group of school girls who were in the house, and told them, "Johnnie Gates and a lot of other boys robbed Mr. Hart's melon patch, and destroyed all they could not carry away." Jost at this moment Johnnie came in whistling, and looking like anything but a thief. "0 girls, get to- gether quick. I've got something for you, and it's 'most school time. The girls looked at each other, and with little movements of disgust turned away. "Why, what's the matter with you all? Hurry up, as the bell will ring," cried Johnnie. "We know what you've got, Johnnie Gates," puke up Sallie, "and we don't want any of your stolen melon ; and I think you should be ashamed of your- self." .. Who says I stole a melon ?" cried Johnnie, in an excited tone. "I guess he'd better not tell me so. I was over at Uncle Henry's Saturday night, and he gave ma a splendid one. and I saved it On purpose to giveyou all some; but, if that is the way you are talking about me, you may do without. " Well, said one of the girls "that is " anyway." at ""Who told you, I'd like to know?" I once, and became so excited, that ebergda, n a nt oy rwhha ent all a " they did not notice that their teacher was in the room until she spoke to Johnnie, asking him to explain the cause of the confusion. Then she carefully examined into the mat- ter until she found that it all came from Kitty Coleman say- ing that she had met Johnnie with a melon. The children who had taken part in the story felt somewhat ashamed of themselves when they saw how much the story had grown in their hands. The teacher said, "I hope every one of you will learn a lesson from this incident, and just now, before the habit becomes fixed, resolve that you will tell nothing but that you know to be true, and that what you do tell you will tell exactly as you heard it; and not tell anything to injure another, even if it is true. I hope Johnnie will for- give you, and that you will never forget the lesson you have learned to-day." I am glad to say that Johnnie did forgive them, and gave them a piece of the melon all around; and I hope that neither they nor aoy of my little readers will grow up ,to be tattling, gossiping men or women._ Mornang-Star. FOREIGN INTLLIGEN3E.
The elections to the Assembly of Notables in Egypt have passed off, it is announced, to the satisfaction of Cherif
Pasha, the Premier: The resignation of the French Ambassadors at Berlin and St. Petersburg is an event of some importance. It is said at _
Paris that M':Challemel Lacour wili go from London to
Berlin and M. Leon Renault to St. Petersburg, the former being replaced at the Court of Bt. James by Count Duchatel.

The cholera is making serious ravages at Mecca. The deaths on the 6th instant amounted to five hundred, and on the next day "it was found impossible to obtain an exact return of the number of fatal cases." The epidemic has also broken out at Djeddah, lilt up to the present time it has not made its appearance on the western shores of tke Red Sea. Guiteau, the assassin of President Garfield, was put upon his trial at Washington, on Monday. There was a very great difficulty in obtaining the services of jurymen who were able to swoar that they had "formed no opinion " on the case, and Glnitean constantly interrupted the proceedings by disorderly exclamations. He is endeavouring to convince the Court that he is insane, but is proceeding on a plan which may produce a result precisely opposite to that which be intends. A correspondent at Berlin telegraphs that it appears hopeless to expect the formation of a working, or even of an absolute, majority in the newly-elected Reichstag. The united Liberal groups, which formerly numbered 129 mem- bers, are.now increased to 160. It is asserted, says a Reuter's telegram, that should Prince Bismarck meet with "systematic opposition" in the Reichstag he will invite Herr von Benningsen and the leaders of the Centre to,take office, remaining himself at the head of the Prussian Government and representing Prussia in the Pederal Council. M. Gambetfa presented himself With his colleagues in the . . .

Government before the Chamber of Deputies ox i Tuesday. The Prime Minister delivered an address to the House, in the course of which ,he said that the Government would seek to advance gradually and wisely in the direction of reform. They would seek to maintain peace at home and abroad; and prominent-, ma—their programme would be the reform of the judicial and educational systems and the com- pletion of the reorganisation of the army. Reference was made in M. Gambetta's speech to the reform of the Consti- tution in order to bring the Senate more in harmony with the popular will. As soon as the speech was concluded, M. Barodet proposed, and M. Clemenceau sunported, a motion demanding, that the revision of the Constitution should be undertaken at once. M. eambetta opposed the motion for" urgency," and it was defeated by 368 votes

• against 120. - An abstract of a spatch addressed by Earl Granville to Sir Edward Malet,l3ritish Consul-General at Cairo, has been published, in which his Lordship reviews the policy of the British Government with regard to Egypt. The despatth is dated November 4. Lord Granville says it cannot be too clearly understood that England desires no Ministry of a partisan character in Egypt. Such a Ministry, founded upon the support of a foreign Power and the personal influence of the diplomatic agent, would not be calculated to serve either the country or the Power in whose interest it might be supposed to be maintained, and could only tend to alienate the native population from their allegiance to the Sovereign, and engender counter intrigues detrimental to the welfare of the State. His Lordship adds that the tie uniting Egypt to the Porte la the best safeguard against foreign Intervention. If it were broken, Egypt might at no distant . date find herself exposed to danger from rival ambitions, The aim of the British Government has been to maintain this tie as it actually exists. The only circum- stance which could force them to depart from the conduct above mentioned would be the outbreaking of anarchy in Egypt, and the Government looked to the Khedive, to Cherif Pasha, and the good sense of the Egyptian nation to prevent such a catastrophe. ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.
HEALTH COMMITTEE.

The first meeting of the Health Committee for the municipal year was held on Friday; Councillor Twyford presiding. There were also present Alderman Gamble Councillors McKechnie, Jamison, Foster, Wilcock, Belsher, and Massey, with Mr. Brewis (town clerk), Mr. J. H. Craik (deputy town clerk), Mr. Hart (borough engineer), Dr. McNicol (medical officer). and Mr. Johnson (borough treasurer).

div.head: INSPECTION OF ALKALI WORKS.
div.p: THE INSPECTION OF ALKALI WORKS.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board saying that, with the view of giving effect to the provisions of the Alkali Works Regulation Act, 1881, the Board was desirous of ascertaining the number of works in the several sanitary districts of England and Wales, and the names of the proprietors or managers of such works. The letter went on to say that an additional inspector of alkali works could , be appointed, provided the Sanitary Authority paid one-half of his salary.—The Cnaiame.w said the question arose when they sent in the return of the works whether they should not ask for un additional inspector. He understood there were to be six inspectors appointed for England and Wales, and he thought he was right in saying that St. Helens did about one-eighth of the alkali trade of England.—Alderman GAMBLE said it was fully one-eighth, as there were works in ,St. Helens not included in that calculation.—Dr. JasusoN moved that the town clerk write for the appointment of one of the additional inspectors.—The TOWN CLERK: They don't say that. You are assuming that they are going 'to appoint more inspectors.—Alderman GAMBLE: I think you may say it is the intention of the Government to appoint additional inspectors, and we from, the trade we do' claim one.—The Tows CLERK : You will probably find that if he Is appoiated entirely by the Government he will not be limited to St. Helens, but will take a larger district.—The CHAIRMAN: I think it would be better to have one paid by the town, so that we can have him about here.—The TOWN CLERK: There certainly is no hartb in asking, but it is a question whether you will get one entirely paid by the Government. Of course, I quite think it right you should get one for the borough of St. Helens.—Dr. JAMISON: We , ought to have one here, but one paid by the Government , will be better, for two reasons: he will save the borough , half the expense, and will be under no suspicion. St. Helens ought to be one district.—The TOWN CLERK said he would draw up a latter, and submit it to the chairman. THE INPECTIOI7S DISEASES HOSPITAL.

The CHAIRMAN : As the Infectious Diseases Hospital is nearly ready to receive patients it will be advisable to say now whether you intend patients to pay for admission, or, if any payment should be made, what amount. That nothing should be charged I do not quite agree with.—The MEDICAL OFEICER Said that if no charge be made there would be no distinction between the Hospital and the Workhouse Infir- mary. Those in the Workhousq would want to 136 to the Hospital. There should be a scale of perhaps from Is. to something upwards. The Whiston Sanitary Authority charged from ss. to £1 per week.—The Diseases Hospital Sub-Committee, consisting of Alderman Harrison, Coun- cillors Belsher, Brook, was requested to take the matter into their consideration and report.—At the request of the Chair- man, Dr. ,kuuisou'o narno was a4do4 to the list of that committee.

CONS TANTINOPLE, TUESDAY.—After Mr. Forster's state- ment in the Financial Commission yesterday, Server Pasha declared'the Finance Minister would make arrangements with the Ottoman Bank to secure a guarantee for the annual payment of £130,000 on the surplus tevenue of Cyprus or on Customs receipts. ENGLAND AND AMERICA.

WASHINGTON, TUESDAY.—At Mr. West's official visit to the White House, yesterday, the British Minister stated to the President that he regarded his reception at Philadelphia as an unmistakable manifestation of the kindly sentiments animating thd American people towards Queen Victoria and Great Britain. The President replied that he had genuine pleasure in heartily reciprocating Mr. West's good wishes personally and officially. The President further spoke of the deep feeling Of friendship and sympathy, between the two countries, and said that the American people would long re- member the many words of affection and sympathy in their recent bereavement from Her Majesty and the people of Great Britain. The United States Government (added President Arthur) would on all points, and at all times, use their best endeavours to promote and develop still more the harmony and goodwill which so signally marks the inter- course between the two nations. The President gave Mr. West a cordial personal welcome.

THE SMOKE NUISANCE: THE NEW TOWN COUNCILLORS. The MEDICAL OFFICER reported :—" Samples of the Eccleston brook branch have been taken by Inspector Wil- liams, at the usual places, between Spray's Bridge and Messrs. Lyon's Bettie works. A faint acid is perceptible in one taken from near Messrs. Daglish's works, but the acidity is lost in the brook lower down, by Messrs. Lyon's Bottle works. Inspector Houghton has taken samples from Hardshaw Brook, at various points. They are free from acid, but the sample taken from the St. Helens chemical drain, where it empties into the sewer in Atlas-street, is not free, but contains acid of less strength than formerly. Since our last meeting I directed the inspectors to take advantage of the empty con- dition of canal and examine the different inlets for works. In carrying out the instructions they discovered drains run- ning acid into the the canal near Messrs. Doulton'i works. In the lower pond, near the double locks, acid was being dis- charged into the,canal from the Globe Alkali works. Since the waters have returned to canal several samples have been taken. There is a slight acid lathe overflow into the brook from the top pond near Messrs. Lyon's Bottle works, and also in the overflow in the lower pond near Merton Bank Bridge. - - - It was a solemn thing to tread over the gronnd,where the most of Christ's Mighty deeds were done—to scramble amid the ruins of a City upon which the woe of the Son of Man' had descended, leaving it for centuries without an in- habitant. This Tell Hum, sometimes called by the Arabs "Capher Nahum " must be the Capernatun of the New , , Teatarnent. Ili spite of authorities such as Robinson and Porter, whose researches in sacred topography are so much valued by all 'Bible students, the mind rests almost ietai- th'e'ree netYaliontbe conviction that you must look for it here, and Laud • Mr. Hepworth Dixon, whose book on the Holy Is ao delightful on account of the side-lights it throws IlPon the scripture records from contemporaneous history, is etrongly of opinion that the weight of evidence is in favour 'lf Tell Huai. He gathers many facts and circumstances from Josenhus in support of the opinion, and then, in turn- ing to the Gospl histories, he thus summarises the evidence Which these afford :—"Caperuaum was a large town, large :no: boats hto be called a city. It lay along the shore of the !alre on iM western bank. It stood near to a creek in which might ride. Bethsaida lay to the north, Magdala to the south of it. The great road from Damascus to Tiberias in through it. In its highest street stood a synagogue, built h ~,-,-Y a Roman °Meer as' 'ft to the Jews; an edifice w`uen, must have been in AT style of art introduced by Herod the Great, with a Grecian portico, having marble columns, cornices, and walls. These points are enough, r when taken together, to constitute proof; and on a closer .o Qin), of the present ruins it will be found that these con- ditions meet in Tell Ruin, and in no other place than Tell ell - ,11121a.r% to We s ee had site to e of Zlng strewn about or heaped one upon another, were frag- twh e d aeal d t hro templeag h t o h re synagogue,lggrasa aanadd there, w' me:lts of a building whose cornices and capitols were in the D st n'3B'ive and ornate style of Grecian architecture. esolation and silence now reign where once the activities of life were ao fervid, where the crowds in the thoroughfares it; wer tit:" the Savicrur to behold His stupendous miracles, . ehdivWd into groups to discuss the wondrous words Which e tha ad fallen from His lips. Igo' the least ap- int nee of storm in sea or sky c mid we discern as we stepped ~ o our boats. All was as smooth, to our impractised eyes, ate when we came down the lake in the morning. We had _round a low promontory that jam out between Tell Hum ~.1.01 5 our destination. In putting out to sea in order to clear '.,1, Point, it became very evident we were in for a squall. th ',Wind Caine rushing down the hills behind us, driving 17e ()oats from the shore and creating great disturbance on oeit'll.tiater. In order to Catch the wind and tack round the c , our boatmen shook out the big sail, but the storm in- LelrrBlng, they soon lost all control of the craft, and were ifiessly struggling to refurl the sail which flapped in the rel'eri while the lost lay ovkr and a capsize seemed in- , hearts as " Save, Lord, i"tr we perish,' was the language of (I),:"eatta as it was of the disciples eighteen hundred years fore; and we owe it to the kind Providence who watched the` tts ln all our journey, that as the storm began to abate, mast and sail were safely lowered into the boat. In the cnotteL boat no such peril had been experienced, on ac- -1,,,,,_"L Or the boatmen keeping all snug. But our friends i,`"l a good deal alarmed, and as the sky still looked angry, t"Rconsented, with ourselves, to push in to the nearest boulders through The boats were pulled in among the , _e ewers, through which the Arab' boatmen had to bear ' It n their hacks. THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 19, 1881.
CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WAiRINGTON.

had given him that reception in con sequence.° f the resolution which had just been passed, namely, that the Government of the late Earl of Beacoosfield—whose death; he believed, even his opponents in this country deeply deplored—did effect wonderful good for this country not only for England itself but also abroad y and that when history came to be written in after ages they would find that all the venom and all the spite which had been heaped on Lord Beaconsfield's name and against his colleagues would have disappeared like chaff before the wind, and that the true grain would then be found and justice would be done to his memory. (Cheers.) With reference to the time at which this meeting was being held there was this advantage in speaking in the month of November. They had had a great number of speeches, letters, and public documents from members of the present Government, and people had begun to find out what had bean before suspected, that there must have been very strong differences of opinion amongst the mei-fiber's of the Cabinet during the last twelve months. He was glad they had had those speeches, and regretted that a good number of them had not been made before and at the time of the last election, and that a good many of those letters and documents had not been before the public then, because he was quite certain if they had a great many people would never have voted as they did, and that the great object which their opponents had at the time, namely, turning the Conservatives out of office, would not have been accomplished. There were two points which formed the great staple of the arguments that were used eighteen months ago, when the Liberals were trying to persuade them that there ought to be a change of Governmsnt. The first of these subjects was the depression of trade. lie was not the least surprised that willing ears should have been open to any charges tending to show that it was owing to the action of the Government of the day thtt they were suffering from these wrongs, and that if there was one thing they wanted to make things comfortable all round it was a change of Government. The present Government had been in power two sessions, and the people had found that trade was not very much better and that wages were not much higher than they were when the Conservative Government was in power. Certain Cabinet Ministers, and the Premier particularly, had endeavoured to account for the present condition of trade, and if those statements had been made at the time of the general election he did not believe that there would have been a change of Government. ( Ap- plause.) Another charge against the Conservative Govern- ment was that they had entirely neglected domestic legisla- tion. The present Government had been in office eighteen months, and they had done very little in the way of domestic legis 'Hon. They bad found, as everybody who studied le4islatlon mast find, that thlre were times and seasons when Governments, however willing to legislate. . ling tin

Tito Conservative electors of South-West Lancashire eesembled in largo numbers in the Public Hall, Wallington, on Tuesday evening, for the purpose of hearing addresses from -Sir Richard Cress and Colonel Blackburn°, the mem- bers for this division of the county. Long before the time ant:minced for the cOnamencement of the proceedings the hall was crowded, and the audience whiled away the time by occasionally singing portions of popular airs which were played upon the organ by Mr. Wm. Johnson. The hall was tastefully decorated, and the platform had a most pleasing appearance. A variety of ferns wore placed in front, and were relieved by an escutcheon of flags in the centre. Im- mediately below the organ were the royal arms adorned with a number of flags. In front of the centre gallery were the , words "Cross and Blackburn for ever," neatly swecuted in orange, in characters that stood out prominently on a blue back ground. On either side of the gallery were the mottoes , "Free trade and fair trade, not fair trade and bad trade," and" Peace with honour, not peace with dishonour," formed in blue letters on a white ground. Shortly after half-past seven, the chairman, Sir Gilbert Greenall, amidst an out- burst of cheering, made his appearance upon the platform, , and was followed by Sir Richard and Lady and Miss Cross, I Colonel Blackbarne and Miss Blackburne, the Hon. L. W. IL Powys and Lady Mary Powys, and there were also on the platform—The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Mr. W.. Beamont, Captain and Mrs. Reynolds, Alderman and Mrs. Shaw Thewlis, Mr. W. H. and Mrs. Brook, Lieut.-Colonel Greene'', Mr. Peter Stubs, Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. J. R. , Buckton, Alderman Joseph Davies, Mr. W. Sharp, Mr. Ai. D. jeans,. Mr. H. B. White, Rev. S. Wilkinson. Rev. E. C: E. Carleton, Rev. W. H. Williams, Rev. J. Ward, Rev. E. St. A. Duke, Alderman Webster, Mr. E. J. Nicholson, Mr. James Tinsley, MreJohn White, Mr. J. Bowes, Councillors J. Pierpoint, W. J. Burgess, RI W. Collin, R. W. Francomb, T. Sutton, and others. The Camases, who was received with cheers, said, Gentlemen,l ain present with you being ODE with with you, and united with you, with very great pleasure. (Hear, hear.) I thank von most heartily and most sincerely for the kind manner in which you have received me and my friends on this occasion—(applause)—and believe me I am not sur- prised that you accept me and my hinds most cordially because we are met together in one mind. (Hear, hear, and a voice "Shout up"; interruption, and cries of "Throw him i out.") We have only one thought, and we have only one future—a determined future. (Hear, hear.) We are deter- I mined that the principles which I hold, and which I believe you hold—(hear, hear)—shall be fearlessly expressed, shall be manfully maintained, and victoriously accomplishee. (Applause.) My friends and gentlemen, I have long desired that we Conservatives should meet. Let there be no mistake on this subject. (Hear, hear.) We are here as Conserva- tives. We are not ashamed of the faith we hold—(cheers) —and we are not undetermined what objects we ititend, with God's blessing, to uphold. (Cheers.) We intend to I stand by the Crown and the dignity of England; and we intend resolutely to maintain those principles, and that creed which placed the present— (Interruption.) lam I glad, most glad, to see so large a meeting. The meeting, gentlemen, is not as large as I expected. (Hear, hear, laughter, and a voice," Where would you put them.'') I mean not as large in the surroundings near me. There are always disappointments. I hoped to have had with us and amongst us a man well known to you—l mean Sir Thomas Edwardes Moss. I expected to have had with me me friend and neighbour, Dr. Mackie. Dr. Mackie, I regret to say, is not able to be present on account of indisposition; and I am sorry, most sorry that yeti have not with you my own kith and kind. I don't believe you will like him the less because he is my nephew. I am sorry Mr. Edward Whitley cannot be present. (Cheers.) Don't mind cheer- ing. lie is worthy your good opinion. (A voice," Be is a gentleman.") He is not here on the present occasion. Ile cannot get here or he would have come. Other engage- ments prevented him. But I have a letter regretting he is not here, and I have tied him fast—l have done my duty— I have tied him fast to a promise that he would be here on two future occasions because he has failed on this . one occasion. (Cheers.) I also regret the unavoidable absence of Mr. Bleckly. Mr. Bleckly is not here in coneequence of , another engagement. Well, now, I have said more than sufficient. Whatever is required to be said will be said by those near me and round me. We have a very large meeting I and a very good attendance. Let us be true to each other. Let us be true to the principles which we maintain. (Claeers.) It is my pleasure and my duty to introduce to you one who will propose the first resolution, a gentleman who has lived long and who has only lived to attain honour, confidence, and affeetion. (Cheers.) Mr. W. BEAMONT moved That this Association fully appreciates the manner in which the Conservative Opposi- tion has fulfilled its arduous and difficult duties in the toHouse of Commons during the past Session, and desires express its unabated confidence in those political Principles which directed the policy of the late Earl of Beaconsfield's Government." He drew atten- tion to two pictures one of England as she was at the beginning of last year, and the other as she was now. In toe first picture they sew that Englasd had averted the threatened war in the east of Europe, and had secured "peace With honour" by the Treaty of Berlin. In Afghanistan our brave army had avenged our wrongs on our perfidious and treacherous foe, and our Indian frontier had been made secure. In South Africa the gallantry of our troops had subdued the Zulus, saved Natal, and given a fair promise of a confederation of the South African pro- vinces which would have assured peace, made them strong ' enough to defend themselves, and proved a great benefit both to the natives and the Colonies. (Cheers.) In Ireland I there was only the usual :hronic disturbances arising out of the lust of land, which the Peace Preservation Act and the I police were able to keep in check. But now, what did we see? In Afghanistan onr gallant army was withdrawn, a I puppet was placed on the throne, and our Indian frontier ' was exposed to the machinations of that empire whose emblem was a two.headed eagle, looking towards Europe and Asia, as if she coveted both. (Hear, hear.) In South Africa we saw nothing but defeat and discomfiture; while I in North Africa one of our near neighbours had possessed herself of Tunis and become an inconvenient neighbour to Egypt. leer treaty of commerce was still unfinished, and ' half threatened to collapse. (Cheers.) Worse than all , this, however, was the state of Ireland, where the Ministers, to buy the Irish vote, declined to renew the Peace Preserva- tion Act; and the result had been the repeal, under another I name, of the Habeas Corpus Act, and the neclssity of send- ing an army into Ireland to prevent, if posaible, such scenes las occurred there in the rebellion of 1798. (Cheers.) For the remedy for these evils they were to look to the great Con- servative party in this country. (Cheers.) To that great I party, under Sir Stafford Northcote, they might confidently look, when the nation returned to her senses again and the Leader of Her Majesty's Opposition changed places with j the Prime Minister. (Cheers.) Alderman Joselm Davin seconded the proposition, and, alluding to the latter part of it, said the name of Beacons- field struck a theme of admiration in their breasts; that , Lord Beaconsfield managed through all the difficulties of a time of universal deprestsion of trade to raise up England to the highest pitch on record upon the brightest page of her bright history, and with the power of a great statesman brought the country to a pinnacle of success she had never previously attained. (Cheers.) Having alluded to ' the foreign policy of Lord Beaconsfield, under whom, he , maintained, the power of England was more admired by our colonies, and who felt more faith in our Government than ever they did before, he adverted to the administration of Ireland by that statesman. He said from 1874 to 1880 Ire- land, that difficult coentry to govern, was in a state of com- parative peace to what she had been, and she became a richer country. than ever she was before. During the time Lord Beaconsfield was working for the benefit of his country, that great man, Mr. Gladstone, writhing under the cold shade of the Opposition, was haranguing the people into what he might call a state of rebellion, and when Mr. Gladstone came into power he found he had so trammelled himself that he was obliged to ally to his Government men unfit to Ibe in the Government of this country. The weak part, as I they often said when they looked at spurious jewellery was Brummagem. The result was that instead of having our Indian frontier protected as Lord Beaconsfield left it, we were receiving news day by day that Russia was nearer and • nearer to her goal. In South Africa we were obliged to admit that our army had been dishonoared, and Ireland was almost in open rebellion. He remarked that the legislation of Ireland bad not been conducted upon proper lines, and hoped for the fntnre they would treat Irishmen as though they were part of this nation. He urged that if we would keep Irishmen as our friends we should have a regal court in ' that country, and suggested that a court should be held in . Dublin on stated occasions. With a view to satisfying the • craving for Home Rule, he would require that the Govern- . ment, as they did in England, should send down commis- sionet s to make personal enquiries on the spot with regard • to local legislation, instead of it being carried to London. He asked them to join with him ite wishing that the day might soon come when Irishmen would be ready ap in the days of yore to fight side by aide with England, and • that both countries might , again win similar victories to • those which had made her name so famous in the past.

If he abused the rules of the House, and it was clear to the com- mon sense of the House that it was for abuse that he Was speaking—that he was not legitimately exercising his right—let him be punished ; but so long as he was exercis- ing his right legitimately and honestly, he ought not to be interfered with. (Hear, hear.) If the Government intended to frame rules which would enable a tyrannical majority to stop the mouth of a member who was honestly saying that which he had a right to say, he (Sir Richard) would with- stand it as long as be had a seat in the House of Comment (Applause.) The time might come and he was not certain whether they were not soon to be in face of it, when an arbitrary Minister, on whatever side, backed up by a I tyrannical majority, if they gave him this power, might do intThite harm and work grievous injustice. If the Govern- ment proceeded on the lines which he had indicated they would receive the cordial support of the-Conservative party. (Applause.) There was another subject about which he could net sit down without saying a few words—he meant I' the question of Ireland. There could be no one there who must not be extremely glad and feel very much relieved • that the Government had at last made up their minds to put their foot down, to try to restore law and order, to preserve life and property, and to show that in all parts of ' the United Kingdom life and personal liberty were the birthright of every free citizen. (Cheers.) They had been called upon by the Prime Minister to support the Govern- ment in the steps they had taken for the support of law and order, and he could honestly say, not only for himself, but also for those with whom he had the honour of acting, that <-0 long as the Government took steps which were neces- sary tor preserving law and order, life,and individual liberty ' they would have their hearty and cordial support. glad to belong to this good old Primitive Methodist ship. Some said they were losing their primitive fire, but he hoped this was not so. Mr. BRAY said that the parting injunction of Jesus to his disciples was to go forth and preach the Gospel. The dis- ciples were to go forth for this purpose throughout the whole world. The Word of the Lord was carried on by in- struments. This always had been, and always would be the case. It was the work of the Church in all ages to preach the Gospel to the world. Had they in their own day been as successful in the work as they had been of old— as the fathers of the Christian Church had been, as their own forefathers were? He pointed to the life and labours of St. Paul as a bright example to the mission workers of all ages. If they had heard Paul preach, they would not have gone away, as he feared they sometimes did now, only half believing. He was a man that preached the Gospel not only with his lips but with his eyes. He preached the forgiveness of sins and life everlasting, and even then the throne of darkness tottered to its fall. It was the truth he preached that brought the Gentiles to the true faith, and it 4as the same Gospel to-day. This Gospel had worked its way through all moral and physical difficulties, and hid triumphed at last. It had done great work in the past, and he trusted it would accomplish even greater thins in the time to come. The Rey. J. PICKWELL also addressed the meeting. But he thought even the subjects treated by Mr. Gladstone himself did not posses the same importance as those in con- nection with the Gospel. He thought there was a lack of interest in these meetings, which he was sorry to see. It was a noble work, and one to which they ought all to lend a helping hand. Jermany, Zuinglius in Switzerland, and John Knox in Scotland, who carried on a glorious and successful war. (Applause.) And the men were there, in the persons of Messrs. Wesley and Whitefield. Judging John Wesley from the standpoint of mental powers, he was a most remarkable min. Did they judge him from the standpoint of hard work? Then he travelled at the rate of 5,000 miles every year, when there were neither railroads nor steamboats. Did they judge him from the standpoint of a writer? Then he wrote almost a library of books, and preached daily to audiences of hun- dreds and of thousands. Did they judge him from the standpoint of heroism and philanthropy? Then, he was bold to say that not in the history of war or in the annals of philanthropy could they find a heroism so lofty, or a philanthropy so pure as that when John Wesley held on a lengthened career in the grand enterprise of seeking souls. Wesley asked for no reward, and at length. died so poor that beyond a well-worn Methodist clergyman's gown, a good library of books, a well-slandered reputation, and the Metho- dist Church—(applause)—he did not leave any- thing more than a few silver spoons and a few pounds in money. Did they judge him from the standpoint of scholarship ? Then early in the University of Oxford he attained to a considerable eminence in learning, and throughout his career he was an omniverous reader in poetry, medicine, and, he was going to say, in almost everything which could at that time be found under the sun. Did they judge of Wesley from the stand- point of sects? Then it was only some 141 years ago, when he said he found peace with God, and his heart strangely warmed, and what had they a few weeks since? An Ecumenical Conference assembled in London in which were representatives of denominations who all acknowledged John Wesley to he their founder, and his theology to be the foundation of their doctrine-24,000.000 of adherents and members—the largest Protestant denomination under the sun; and they would say—To God be all the glory! Did they judge him from the standpoint of posthumous influ- ence? Then the way in which he was praised and blamed; the way in which some critics awarded him almost spot- I less virtues, and the numerous biographies that were so frequently written about him, surely stamped him as no ordinary man; and proved that amongst the influences i whin moved society today that of John Wesley must be considered a very powerful one indeed. (Loud applause.) Mr. Hack then dwelt with the chief biographical facts in the life of Whitefield; his birth in 1714 at the city of Gloucester' in the Bell Inn, which was kept by his mother, I and where he acted as waiter when a youth; his association with the Wesleys at Pembroke College, Oxford; his early sermons, which proved wonderfully successful; his visit to Georgia and bisf oundation of the Orphan House; his return to England; the closing of the church doors against him when he took to field preaching, and addressed vast multitudes; his other visits to America, and the manner in which his eloquence caused even the philosophic Franklin to empty his pockets into the collection box ; his addresses in the Countess of Huntingdon's drawing room, when Lord Chesterfield and Bolingbroke were his hearers, and his final death from asthma at Newbury—port in New England, America. During the course of his remarks the lecturer, whilst complimenting the Bishop of Liverpool and many of the Clergy of the Established Church on the evangelical doctrine which they preached, said that, at the same time, he did not see that the Weeleyans could go back to the Church of England. He thought that God, by the remark- able history he had given the denomination in the past, by the fact that in these days of bankruptcy and bad trade they could raise £300,000 for the consolidation and exten- sion of their work—(applause)—and by the fact that the Ecumenical Council represented so large a constituency, and went in, in its spirit and purpose at any rate, for noble work—these facts maraed them out as a church designed by God for a distinct mission; that they were not to be influ- enced by politics; that they were to he "the friends of all and the enemies of none ;" and that their one grand mission was to associate themselves with the other evangelical churches, and try to bring the world to the footstool of the Saviour. (Loud applause, and a 'oice: Amen.) White- field's elocution and general oratorical power was something wonderful. To quote the words of another (Dr. Punshon), "Xis power of description must have been marvellous. Men . .

THE RIGHT HON. JOHN BRIGHT'S 70TH BIRTHDAY. In Rochdale, on Wednesday, the 70th birthday of Mr. Bright was celebrated with great enthusiasm; bunting was displayed on every hand, and there were triumphal arches in various parts of the principal thoroughfares. In the afternoon a deputation from Mr. Bright's Birmin,tham con- stituents dined with him at his residence, One As. tnd there presented him with ea address in which they ref.. red red with pride to his long connection with their borough, and promised him unabated confidence and support during the remainder of his life. Later in the day Mr. Bright's workpeople presented him with another address, conveying their deep respect and affection for him, and referring in terms-of heartfelt gratulation to his many services to his country. Mr. Bright graphically compared the present condition of the working classes with their past, descanted upon the benefits of education, and described the Education Act as one of the most blessed improvements of modem times. At the evening meeting in the Town Hall, Mr. Bright's recep- tion was wildly enthusiastic, he was presented with a handsomely-illuminated address. Ia reply, Mr. Bright con- fined his observations principally to free trade and the benefis it has conferred on the working classes, and showed that, even with an incsease of ten millions of population since 1840, hours had been shorter, wages higher, employ- ment steadier, and the general condition of the people vsstly better. On the land question, he said unless means -were taken to stimulate the production of the soil by the in- creased capital and skill put into it, there was no remedy whatsoever for the farmers' suffering and distress, but a great and permanent reduction of the landlords' rents There were torchlight processions, bonfiles, and fireworks at night.

div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE.—The amount of business doing in the iron trade during the past week has been com- paratively limited. Pig iron meets with a very dull sale, consumers, who are mostly well covered for the present, pre- ferring to wait the turn of the year, but with the exception of a few low-priced parcels of outside brands which have come into the market under exceptional circumstances, late rates are well maintained, makers themselves showing no disposition to give way. Lancashire makers of pig iron would now be open to book orders up to March next at their full rates of 48s. to 495., less 21, for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, but there are very few inquiries coming in. Heavy deliveries are, however, still being made on account of old contracts, and these take away the present output. Finished iron continues in fair demand for the time of the year, and in some quarters there is an expectation of large American orders before long coming into this district. Local makers, who are full at orders for the present, are very cautious about booking forward, and although there is some underselling on the part of dealers they are firm at £6 10s. to £6 159. for bars delivered into the Manchester district. Founders, engineers, and tool makers are fairly busy, but there is not so much activity amongst machinists. LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.—There has been but a very dull demand during the week for all classes if round coal used for bouse-fire purposes, and colliery proprietors, who are now rapidly working off the order left on hand at the close of last month, in some cases are finding it difficult to move off their present output where the pits are working full time. At many of the collieries up in the West Lancashire district, however, as the result of the recent decision to restrict the output, the men are working only irregularly. Here and there prices are slightly easier, but as the present lull in the demand is due largely to the exceplonal mildness of the weather and consequently may be only temporary, there is generally a disposition at present to stock rather than give way upon late rates, and at the pit mouth quota- tions remain at about 103. for best coal, with seconds house coal averaging about Bs. Bs. 6d. per ton. For common round at the pit mouth the average price is about 7s. per ton, for good burgy 59., and for slack from 3s. to 45. per ton, accord- ing to quality. Shipping has been rather quiet, and prices, if anything, easier ; good steam coal averaging about to Be 3d. at Garston, and Be. 6d. per ton at the high level. Liverpool.
There were 4,450 pawnbrokers this year, licensed a £7 105., producing £33,375.

He claimed 10 per cent, as commission.—His Honour gave judgment for the defendant to pay to the plaintiff the amount for which he sold the potatoes, less commission, and remarked that he did not doubt the trans- action was one of commission. , A FRODSHAM FARMER AND HIS RENT.—PSIST Roberts, Hapsford, Frodsham' claimed from James Mort, Kingsh v, the sum of £3 for balance of rent.—The plaintiff said defendant rented a small farm from him at a yearly rent of £4O. On the 25th March last he received from the defen- dant £l7, which was £3 less than the half-year's rent—The defendant said that when he took the farm the defendant promised to give £lO to make certain improvements to fences. He bought a lot of new stumps and improved the farm "7 much, and now be declined to give him the £lO. —The plaintiff said the arrangement was that he should give the defendant SIO if he sold the farm at a large profit, but instead of that he lost £2OO by it.—His Honour said that as defendant had not brought forward a witness who, he professed, could have cleared up the matter, he had no other course open but to give a verdict for the plaintiff.

CREWE ALEXANDRA T. TALE lixxosits.—The above Association clubs met, for the first time this season, on Saturday last, at Talke. Both clubs put in the field their best teams, with a alight exception, and after an hour's play the Alexandras were declared the winners by three goals to one. The game was fast, and well contested throughout. RUNCORN WHITE STAR V. WIDNES WEVIT STAR —This

- match was played on the ground of the former at Runcorn, and, after a most pleasant and evenly-contested game, Run- corn White Star proved the victors by a disputed try, Kirkham, Tickle, and Fletcher playing well for Runt:ern. Score: Runcorn, 1 dasputed 14, 4 touchdowns, and 1 dead ball, to Widnes 1 teach in goal.
