Percival ; forwards, W. Clare, A. Clare, Mullany, Lancaster, Button, Cox, Snowball, Ridgway, Brett. BIRKENHEAD RANGERS f. RL'ICCORN.—The above Oahe met, for the first time, on Saturday last, on the ground of the former, and after a very pleasant game ended in atLeasy victory for the visitors, who played a remarkably rrood game; Wright, Bennett, Cox, Atherton, being to the front as forwards, while nothing can be said in particular about the backs, as all played a good sure game. For the home team, S. Lea, J. Cullaton, D. Walton, forwards; A:Fisher, W. Doyle, backs, played well. Runcorn, one goal, three tries, five touchdowns, one touch in goal, to nil. The, fol. lowing are the teams: Birkenhead Bangers: 8,.. Price;, full back; J. Brocklebank, J. Price, three-quarters: W. Doyle, A. Fisher, half-bacbs ; C. Hall, D. Walton, W. Huxley, S. Lea, J. Snape, R. Heague, D. Edwards, J. Landon, J. Sackett, J. Callaton. Runcorn: F, Joule, full back; F. Roach, H. Hughes, W. Larkin. three-quarters; W. Broady, H. Andrews, half-backs; W. Wright, J. Gatley, L. Crosby, W. Riley, J. Lewis, W. Cox, H. Atherton, W. Bennett, T. Bate (captafe). RUNCORN V. Sr. HELENS RECREATION (2ND TEAMS).— These teams met at Runcorn on Saturday, when a pleasant gains was witnessed. The Runcorn captain winning the toss, the visitors started the ball with the wind in their favour, followed up, and play ensued in Runcorn 25, when W. Pownall quickly relieved by a good run, which Grittens improved by running in and gaining the first try, which Sherlock converted into a goal. On drop out the Same team forwards kept the ball in the Recreation 25, in spite of the desperate efforts of Valentine to get away, when Dun- bavand again crossed the visitors' line. The kick at goal, however, failed. Play was now carried on in neutral ground, and when half-ti toe was called the visitors had not scored. Mason re-started the ball with the wind in his favour, andit was returned by Conway. Dean got possession, and by a dodgy run carried the ball well into the visitors' qsarters, when W. Pownall, who had bees conspicuous by some spirited play, grounded the ball across the visitors' line; no goal, however, resulting. The Recreation being rather slow in touching the ball dead, the home team got on the ball again, and Gittens nicely managed to place another try to the credit of his side. The place kick, however, failed. Some good dribbling was now and again affected by Denni- son and Dunbavand, who played splendidly together throughout the game. By combined effort the home team forwards rushed up again to the Recreation lines, Dunbavand scoring another try; the kick at goal, thou4/i a good attempt, failed. The visitors now tried hard to make up for their leeway, Valentine making some good runs, but Sher- lock's safe tackling was all that could be desired. Play Again ensued in the visitors' 25, when they began to act on the defensive and touched down. The ball being brought into play, Valentine got possession and made a good attempt to get through his opponents, when Clarke safely tackled him, going into touch in Runcorn 25, when Powns all made a smart run and,cieared,the lines. Dennison and Dunbavand dribbling the bail into Runcorn 25, when Denni- son gained another try; the place kick, being a difficult one, failed. The visitors struggled hard to avert a defeat, but the home team could not easily be pushed off; and Mason seemed like another another score, when he was tackled on the goal line, and a maul ensued, ending in favoar of the visitors, who touched down. The ball being put in motion, a scrimmage WAS formed in visitors' 25, when ;Mason got possession and crossed the lice; the place kick, which was a good attempt, failed, a little more judgment I being required in the placing of the ball. Scrimmun was formed again, when Mason again placed another try to the credit of his side. No side being called left the Runcorn ' the victors by 1 goal, 7 tries, 4 minor points, to St. Helens nil. Clarke, Dennison Riley, Masm (cap' ,in), Dunbavand, Dean, Wninyates, Vainwright, and J. Ki-kharn, forwards. St. Helr ns: Nicol and Westhead, fell-backs; Valentine, Seddon, and Bold, three-quarter hacks; Cone , and Robinson, half-backs; liyam, Carlisle, Ellison, Moly. neaux, Fernley, Marsh, Hammond, and another forwards.

Where will he find, in the speeches of that time, a tihagle denial by responsible speakers on the Liberal Side that there had been "bad harvests ? " Cabinet Ministers do say now that there had been bad seasons for farmers and want of sun ; but we may challenge roundly the remark that these statements contradict 'what they said eighteen months ago when in opposi- tion. An enormous majority of the electors deliber• ately endorsed at the General Election Lord Harting- ton's exceedingly temperate statement that the flat- ness of trade had been " aggravated " by the Tory fereigil Policy of unrest, aggression, and intrigue. Sir Richard Cross has to confess that tacitly, whilst :fad a cotru se he greatly laments it. But he tries to think, 'lake his friends believe, that the electors have abaci) seen their mistake, and are coming to a better rain& We should really like to know what minutest atom of Proof has been furnished by subsequent events that the electors' conclu42ns, at the elections of 1880, were wrong. There have intervened two Years more of singulaily disastrous weather for the laEirvest time of this country. Liberal Governments, tclnallY with Conservative, have to encounter the drawbacks to public prosperity by sunless summers and Alined crops. In spite of that, trade has unquestion- ably improved in most branches; and Liberals are entitled to say that the evil effects of deficient harvests bave not been" aggravated" by the action of the new Cl°l'erlarnent abroad or at home, but have been visibly mitigated. Here then we have the startling fact that whereas the places of worship have increased in the space of thirty years from 15 to 29, and the population from 22,984 to 40,960, the number of per- sons attending places of worship has decreased from 13,442 to 13,286 ! This is a subject worthy of the careful consideration of every thoughtful person. What is the cause of this declension, and why is it that the great masses of the people are to be regarded as not attending any placo of worship whatever. The poptlation has almost doubled itself in this generation, the number of religious bodies in Warrington have in- creased, and the number of places of worship have in- creased to nearly double their number in 1851 ; and yet in spite of increased educational facilities and all the religious agencies at work in the town, the figures before /is slow, a very great decrease in the per- centage of per sonsattending religious places of worship. The statistical return for Runcorn shows that with a population of 15,000 there were 19 places of worship with a morning attendance of 3,229, and afternoon and evening of 6,418, giving a total of 9,647. If we take from these figures these attending the Salvation Army meetings, we find that the attendance at the regular churches and chapels only amounts to 6,688 persons, or less than one-half the entire population. It will, therefore, be seen that our remarks with re-
ference to the great majority being non-attendants at places of worship apply with equal force to that town as well.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

It appears that in my remarks a few weeks ago concerning Mr. Annett, the master of Holy Trinity School, Runcorn, I proved a sort of prophet, for a movement has taken place within the past two months which was evidently intended to work no good to that gentleman. Some of the critics of Mr. Annett at the School Board put themselves together and wrote a letter to the Education Department, drawing the attention of their lordships to an alleged " discrepancy " between the figures supplied to the Department during the ' late dispute and those sent in to the School Board. A reply was forwarded to the effect that if the members of the School Board had discovered any such "discrepancy" it was their business to point it nut to the master at Trinity schools, "for they (their lordships) had nothing to do with ' the matter." Thus ends, at least as far as the present is concerned, "this strange, eventful history." On hearing of this little story, I was somewhat puzzled to find, on refer- ring to the report of the last meeting of the Board, that there was no reference to the letter; but I have since been informed that the communication was handed round to the members for inspection, bat was not read, so that Tour representative's silence on the subject is explained. The question arises of how it was that this interesting bit of correspondence was not allowed to see the light. I admire the use of the word " discrepancy " in the communication, as.it is a far preferable one to "false statement." Sometimes men grow wiser as they grow older.

The numerous friends of the Rev. George Holloway, vica of Farnworth Parish Church, will regret to hear that he is leaving the neighbourhood, having exchanged his living with a gentleman in Norfolk. Those who have read the works of the American hurnoar- ist, who has written somewhat at length on the vagaries of "my friend the tramp," will have noticed that that worthy person is not without a sense of quiet humour, which no doubt at times somewhat relieves the monotony of his existence. Tramps do not receive a very hearty welcome at Dution Workhouse; and I am told that upon the door of the casual ward are a uumber of inscriptions ia pencil, some of which are of so amusing a character that they would prove quite a godsend to that, at times, very dreary London publication known as Punch. As a sample I give the following :

"lie who Calls and stops at Dutton, Will never dine on beef or mutton!" The friends of the Establishment in Whines will be pleased to hear that the land at Anderton's corner has been transferred, and it is stated that the work of erecting the new church will Positively be commenced within the next three months.

It must be very gratifying to the Nonconformists of this town to see how well their strength in the town was revealed by the light of the religious census which appeared in the Exantiner of last week. The day has gone by when clergy- men can, afford to give the cold shoulder to Nonconformist ministers, many of whom have taken the highest degrees which it is in the power of the noblest seats of learning the land to confer.

It will be remembered byyour readers that at the time of the terrible accident at the Widnes Foundry crossing, by which two men lost their lives, some very severe remarks were made by the county coroner (Mr. C. E. Driffield), concerning the laxity of the London and North-Western Railway Co., In not being sufficiently active in proocuting offenders who trespassed on the line. The castigation appears to have had the effect of causing the company to take more determined steps than in the past, and to prosecute any one who per- sists, after being once warned, in trespassing. At the Wid- nes Police Court, on Monday, two men were found to have been guilty of going upon the line near the crossing, after being warned, and were each ordered to pay 10s. This will, in all probability, make them a little more cautious in future and also act as a warnieg to others who may be inclined to fellow their silly example.

I imagined that the days when it was found impossible to get above one justice of the peace to attend at Widnes Petty Sessions had gone for ever, since the number of magis- trates had been so largely increased; but on Wednesday several of the cases had to be adjourned owing to the fact that the only representative of Her Majesty present on the bench was Mr. H. S. Hall.

Judging from the reports I hear on every side, there is some danger that the local parliament at Runcorn will shortly become a thing of the past, if those who in previous sessions have taken such a lively interest in its proceedings, do not try to increase the number of members. The young men of the Conservative party are said to be to blame, as so comparatively few upon that side of the House put in an appearance. Are we to take this as a proof that the majority of the intellectual "young lions" in the town have become co averts to the principles of Liberalism, or are the Tories so downhearted at the success of the Gladstone Government that they have lost all pluck? Runcorn has not too many attractions for young men, and it will be a pity if the society becomes extinct. At the last annual meeting of the Amateur Bicycle Club a statement was made that there was not so much interest taken in the proceedings of the association as in years gone by. An attempt was made to account for this fact by a statement te the effect that some of the members were getting too Falstaffian in their proportions to find that pleasure which they formerly did in bicycling, and that others had got married. Coupled with the complaints of the want of interest shown in the Debating Society, it seems as if many of the young men in the town were be- coming too much like Tennyson's lotos eaters, and had a great desire to take things far too easily. I understand that Mr. D. Swift, who is so well known on what may be described as the St. Helens and Widnes police circuit, is at present "eating his dinners" in London, pre- paratory to being called to the bar as a barrister upon the northern circuit. Many of Mr. Swift's professional brethren speak very confidently concerning the assured success of that gentleman as a wearer of "the long robe." Why should St. Helens not have its resident barrister as well as other towns?

Press would do good if they "pitched into " the. now. I I heard it said the other day that they who wraitbesufroarittihese of the fashions to which the fair sex are slaves just quite agree with the gentleman referred to, that the vagaries Of fashion ought to be written down, but I scarcely think that the opinions of the " lords of creation will weight with the ladies in this matter. Old men Can remember how much was written and spoken against such absurdities in years gone bye; but it was all to no purpose, for ladies would continue to persist in wearing crinolines, Grecian bends,&c., to their own discomfort, until llikaeve myselflnuch the fashion changed. There cannot be two opinions as to the ridiculousness of seeing a young lady tied round so tightly that if she falls she cannot get up again. But what will my readers say about that fair maiden who is such a slave to fashion that the other day she found herself unable to reach the knocker of the door a the house she was visiting, and was therefore obliged to ask a good Samaritan who was passing to help her in the dilemma ? I would advise such never to go out without a footman, else, if she should happen to fall down some frosty morning she will be in a sad plight. I understand that Mr. W. J. Davies, the energetic secre" tary of the Runcorn Starr-Bowkett Society, is resigning his position, and that Mr. Wm. Handley has consented to be- come his successor.

The annual meeting of the members of the United Cheshire and Lancashire Permanent Benefit Building Society, at Runcorn, last week, was a fairly satisfactory one, consider- ing the late very dull times. A dividend was declared at the rate of four per cent., and a hearty vote of confidence passed in the officers of the association, on the proposition of the Vicar of the Parish, seconded by the Rev. W. Preston. I am assured by several gentlemen, whose judgment is worth having, that the only thing needed to place this society in the enviable position which it once occupied is a little Patience, without which it is hard to accomplish anything of importance. FLACCUS,
'MGM

div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 19, 1881.
DrrroN IRONWORKEL—We understand that there is a
prospect of these works being re-opened under new manage- ment.

VICTORIA-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—A series of special mission services are being held during the present week at this chapel. On Sunday the Rev. J. H. Cummings occupied the pulpit morning and evening, and on Monday the Rev. J. Hathersall preached. It is proposed during the week to hold special mission services in connec- . . . . . .
_ tion with the chapels in various parts of the town for the benefit of the working people.

Rtmcons Rua AL SANiTARY Amraonsmr.—There were present at the meeting of this Authority, held at .Ditton, Workhouse, on Tuesday, the Revs. Canon Barclay (chair- man), J. W. N. Tanner, Rigby, Knowles, Ashton, Andrews Mkiwood, James Darbyshire, and Whitlow.—Dr. J. G. Bride, the medical officer, reported the outbreak of scarlet fever in the township of Ashton Heath. Mr. Farrington's three children had been attacked•with the disease, which appeared to have been imported from the neighbourhood of Halton Lodge, Halton, by the father during the performance of his duty as nuisance inspector. All the cases were doing well, and disinfection had been fully carried out. Whooping cough had broken out at Whitley Superior, arid one death had resulted.—Mr. Bancroft, the engineer, reported that the works at the outfall of the Frodsham sewerage scheme was progressing, and in six weeks would probably be completed. —The doctor's report was adopted.

WESTON SONS OF TEMPERANCE. - The Nil Des- perandum Division of Sons of Temperance had a very successful meeting on the night of the nth inst. at Weston, under the presidency of Mr. Ho'ford. The Church school- room was well filled by an audience in deep sympathy with the movement, which appears to have taken a firm root in the village. The Chairman referred to the main objects of the society, which were to shield its members from the . . . _

, temptation and the evils resulting from intemperance; and to afford assistance in time of sickness or accident. Ile first result was effected by the adoption of the total absti- nence pledge, and severing the members from the multipli- city of evils attendant upon meetings held at public-houses. Mr. Holford quoted from the statistics prepared by Mr. Nelson, which showed that in other societies the average sickness was 283 per cent., and the death-rate 12.63 per 1,000; while in the London Grand Division of Sons of Temperance the average sickness was only 1.34 per cent., and the deasth-rate 5.77 per 1,000. Other temperancel organizations showed similar results, and he contcnded that if a change were made in non-abstaining secitties, and they adopted the temperance principle, that their death-rate would decrease by one-half. The programme was then com- menced by the fife baud belonging to the order, who very well played one of their selections from their musical repertory. The Brunswick glee party enhanced very much the enjoyment of the evening's proceedings by their tasteful rendering of several glees and a part song, in which Miss Horton and Messrs. It. Bit kett and It. Morris took part. Mr. J. Moulton read "The bashful man" in a very humorous style. Miss Horton and Miss Jones deserve much praise for the conspicuous ability with which they performed their parts of the programme. Mr. J. rownall was listened to with great pleasure, and he did full justice to the " Lullaby" song, for which he was encored. Mr, Fred. Nickson was very amusing in his humorous song, "The boat's a going over," and ''he also was mimed. Mr. It. Morris was deservedly encored in the song The nthishipmite." 'The duet, "Courtship," given by Miss Horton and Mr. Mon is, was worthy of the applause with which it was received. Mr. John Ravenscroft assisted as accompanist.

UNDER TILE PALMS.—MUSICAL PERFORMANCE AT RUNCORN.—On Tuesday and Wednesday evenings Mr. G. F. Root's sacred cantata, entitled " Under the Palms, or the Jewsb Flower Feast," was given in the school-room of the United Methodist nee Clutch, Runcorn, to large audiences. About 50 people, including about 30 children, took part. The platform was very tastefully decorated with evergreens and plants, including several varieties of the palm fern, lent by Mrs. Chat les Hazlehtirst. The evergreens had been brought from Frodsham and the neighbourhood by Mr. Richard Moore, and the tif:dattlollB had been put up by the members of the choir, the teachers in the school, and other friends. This is the first occasion Upon which the cantata has been given in the town; and we may mite that it was composed by Mr. G. F. Root, of Chicago, U.S. One of the leading features in connection with it is that it is of such a description that horn the youngest child up to the adult, all may take part in the performauce. The events depicted in the first part of the composition relate to the rettun of the Jews from their captivity in Babylon, and the journey from the city of hanging gardens to Jerusalem, including the 'various stoppages on the way, are depicted in Wautiful song and chorus. The socond part consists of an account of the holding of the Feast of Tabernacles, which commemorated the ingathering of the harvest, and was at this particular time given under the direction of the prophets Ezra and Nehe- miah. From the account in the Book of Nehemiah, it ap- pears that booths were set up on the roofs, the court-yards of the house, in the courts of the temple, and even in the Holy City itself. It is stated that from the days of Joshua, the son of Nun, until the return from captivity, the Jews had not kept the feast. The choruses were given with g:eat effect, especially the one by the little children, entitled " Little ones of God are we," which, in revonse to an encore, was repeated on the second night of the performance. Mrs. Isfewall sang the solos alotted to her very tastefully, and amongst them were "0 shepherd, who leadest," and " We remembered the graves of our fathers." The solo quartett by Mrs. Cutzion Carr, and Messrs. Jones, Williams, and T. Moore was executed in a very commendable manner. Some of the tenor solos were very indifferently sung, and the bass might have been improved. However, considering that the performers were amateurs, we feel quite justified in saying that the whole went off very creditably indeed. Mr. John Holford proved a good conductor, and Miss Clough presided at the harmonium very effectively. We believe that the proposal to have such a performance in aid of certain im- provements carried out for the convenience of the choir, originated with Mr. Holford, and much praise is due to him for the pleasant manner,in which the entire affair passed off.

RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBITING SOCIETTY.— Owing to the unavoideble absence of the Speaker at the weekly meeting, on Tuesday night, the Solicitor-General was voted to the chair.—The Leader of the Opposition asked whether it was the intention of the Government to keep Messrs. Parnell and Dillon in Kilmainham until the expira- tion of the Coercion Act in Miy, IBs2.—The Premier seid Awes certainly a. very definite question, but it would admit of several answers and amongst those a very simpte one. It was not the intention of Her Majesty's Government to keep Messrs. Parnell and Dillon in Kihnainhatn until the expira- tion of the Coercion Act. Fle thought it was within the knowledge of the Government and other members of the Hone that arrangements had been made for the removal of these two men along with other suspects to various gaols in Ireland. It was obvious to everyone that the liberty of these gentlemen had been, and was still in their own hands by re- fraining from offending law and justice, and also from using words tending to stir up strife and seeitfon. If to avoid these acts they would pledge their word and honour, they would be liberated at once.—The member for Swansea resumed the debate on the Queen's speech. Dwelling on the fourth clause, he said that the way in which matters were working in Ireland proved that the hope mentioned has not been void of foundation.—The member for Nottingham contended that the Government should have passed the Coercion Act as soon as they came into power. He said Lord Beaconsfield prophesied all this would come to pass. Lord Beaconsfield himself spoke of the state of Ireland as that of veiled rebellion. The reason was under pressure of evictions caused by famine the tenants got no compensation for disturbance, and the people were in such a state that the speeches of the Land Leaguers excited and drove them into a state of desperation. The Government seeing their condi- tion, proposed to pacify them by enquiring into the state of the land law and passing a measure for the relief of tenants who were evicted. The Land Commission had proved that Ireland had her grievances. The Government remedied one of them when they gave them Catholic Emancipation ; another at the Disestablishment of the Irish Church ; and now they had carried a Land Bill. Many of the rents had been reduced from 20 to 30 per cent. Honourable' gentlemen opposite would call that spoliation, but he con- tended it was not spoliation for they were simply taking back the plunder which the landords had robbed them of in the past. Thanks to the Liberal Government, the farmers were now in a position to reap the labours of their lands.— The Chancellor of the Exchequer said the only argument which bad emanated from the side of the Opposition, and. which carried with it any weight, appeared to be the doubt- ful character of the Speech. Ile maintained that their hope was not forgotten in despair. What they had done in the past bid them to hope in the future.- They had striven, and were striving to help those around them.—An interval of five minutes took place whilst the Leader of the-Opposition hunted up some of his supporters ; but as no one seemed to be prepared for a speech, the member for Edinburgh City rose and spoke in support of the Gonernment policy.—The Leader of the Opposition drew attention to a member sitting with his hat on ; he thought that in deference to the Speaker that member should remain uncovered.—The member for Chelsea held that members could remain with their hats on after having taken their seat, but when walking in front of the Speaker, or crossing the floor, it was against the rules of the House, which was confirmed by the Speaker.—After some further discussion the Speech was passed without dis- sent.—The Leader of the Opposition wished to know what was the course of business the Ministry intended to pursue. —The Premier replied that he would beg leave for the Home Secretary to introduce a Bill celled the" Removal of Parlia- mentary Disabilities Bill," which was agreed to, and read by the clerk.—The member for Nottingham afterwards proposed that "this Bill be not introduced at the present time, which caused a great commotion.—The member for Birken- head thought the Government had a right to introduce Bills without asking leave of the House, but the Speaker ruled that no measure should be set down for discussion without that permission, and that no objection to the introduction could afterwards be entertained.—The Leader of the Opposi- tion said he had great pleasure in seconding the proposition. " This bad the effect of bringing three or four members at once to their feet, and callingthe Speaker's attention to the motion manner in which the Opposition were trying to " work a Point," by rejecting the measure, or, in other words, giving A negative vote.—After considerable excitement and Aries of chair, chair," the ru. le, the time 9-45 p.m had expired and he would put the as to the Speaker introduction seatede of tbe Be that t a s accordingalready d y the rk to the H etaotbh Cle e House, which was eventually carried.— Amidst much uproar and disorder the House rose.

THE ST. AMBROSE LCHITRCH BAZAAR.—The total SUM realised at this bazaar was £5Bl, which will, it is stated, be sufficient to pay off the debt of £2OO upon the church, and to provide the £2OO for thet repair fund, which must exist before the building can be consecrated. RUNCORN BRANCH OF THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEM- PERANCE SOCIETY.—On Sunday, the Rev. T. Storey-Bates, organising secretary of the Church of England Temperance Society, preached a sermon in the Runcorn Parish Church on behalf of the organisation, which realised upwards of Ze. RUNCORN MADRIGAL CLUB'S CONCERT.—The members of this club will give "The Creation," at the Public Hall, on Monday evening. The principals include Madame Bel- linie Porter (whose singing at the Widnes Choral Society's concert on Thursday evening was much admired), Mr. J. J. Hodson, and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint. HALTON RIVTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. —Oa Tiles- evening, Mr. John Miller read a paper to the members of the society on "The Jewish Religion." Mr. A. E. Davies occupied the chair, and the following gentlemen took part in the discussion: Messrs. J. Gamon, G. Penington, R. Hughes, and J. Haddock. There was a fair attendance of members. CATHOLIC ENTERTAINMENT AT APPLETON.—An entertain- ment in connection with St. Bede's Catholic Chapel, Apple- ton, took place on Monday. The Rev. Father Finegan presided. The concert was a varied and agreeable one, and the programme of popular melodies was gone through in a thoroughly artistic manner. The concert did not rely solely upon local talent, though the name .f Mr. J. Morrison is a guarrantee that the vocalists of Widnes were not unrepre- sented. On the contrary, the services of Mr. Josef Cantor, well known to the patrons of the Liverpool Hope Hall con- certs, and Miss Madrene and Nono, both also ot LiYerpool, had been secured, and their efforts met with a hearty and well-deserved appreciation. There was a good audience, and they evidently relished the excellent musical fare provided for them. The proceeds of the concert were devoted to the the funds for the enlargement of: the Appleton Catholic schools.

HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SO. CIETY.—The second meeting in connection with the above society was held in the Girls' school on Monday, when the Rev. J. Lockwood (vicar) was the essayist. The chair was

taken by Mr. Stokes, vicar's warden, and there was an ex- cellent attendance of members. The subject, which the essayist termed " Reminiscences of his visit to France," was most interesting and instructive, and was thoroughly appreciated by all present. Mr. D. Baguley proposed, and Mr. Brown seconded a vote of thanks to the Vicar for the kind and able manner in which be had entertained them.— It was proposed by Mr. Wright, and seconded by Mr. G. Grute, Ben., that the thanks of the meeting be also rendered to Mr. Stokes for occupying the chair.—Both resolutions were adopted. A FACT FOR THE TEMPERANCE SOClETY.—Drunken- ness does not appear to be decreasing in Warrington; for at the Police Court, on Monday, 19 persons were convicted of that unlawful practice. Of this number about 10 had been arrested on the Saturday and Sunday previous. TRIG WA.REINGTON TRAGEDy.—The Austrian, Edward Scholtze, who was a few weeks ago clmmitted to the Liverpool Assizes, on the charge of attempting to murder his wife, is too weak to stand his trial, which has been con- sequently postponed untirthe next assizes. STREET ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON.—WhiIat MT. A MynekYme, butcher, was transacting business in the post office, on Thursday morning, the horse which he had left in his cooveyance outside took fright, and ran at a furious rate down Sankey-street. Near Market-gate a man attempted to stop the infuriated animal by drawing his hurry across the road, but it ran on the footpath, and got past. Near the Brittania Inn, Buttermarket-street, the conveyance came in contact with a handcart, and was overturned, throwing the horn to the ground. No damage was done, and the horse is but slightly injured. PRESENTATION AT WARRINGTON.—To show the respect and esteem in which Mr. Robert Young is held by the members of the Warrington Wiredrawers' Society, of which he was secretary, they presented to him a capital painted portrait of himself, on Monday evening. On the frame of the portrait there is inscribed :—"Presented to Mr. Robert Young by the Wire Drawers', Society on the occa- sion of his marriage, July 14th, 1881, as a token of their respect and esteem for services rendered to the above society." Mr. John Reynolds made the presentation, and Mr. Young, in replying, thanked the members for their kind appreciation of his services. EXTRAORDINARY SUICIDE AT WARBINGION WORK- motrsE.—Early on Thursday morning an inmate of the Warrington Workhouse, named John Eyes, 70 years of age, succeeded in putting an end to his life. He had for some time back been confined to his bed of a serious illnees, and each [light had been tended by another pauper. He seemed however, to have evaded the vigilance of his attendant, for at 1-30 on the morning named, he cut his throat, severing the jugular vein. His instrument was the blade of an old table knife, with two pieces of wood tied together with twine for a handle, and very blunt. lie must have possessed con- siderable resolution to do tie deed with such a weapon. He died before the arrival of the:doctor, 'who had bLen sum- moned. Heyes had been an inmate of the house more or less for the last 18 years. He is stated to have been a very desparate character, and was a retdrned convict. WIDNES .CHORAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.—The members of the Widnes Choral Society gave their first concert for the season in the Volunteer Hall, on Thursday, the oratorio selected being the difficult one of "Judas Maccabeeus." The principals on Thursday evening were Madam Billinie Porter, Miss Davies, Mr. J. J. Hodson, and Mr. H. Cuzner. Mr, W. I. Arent was conductor. We regretted to see so small an attendance, the room not being half full. The manner in which the difficult music was rendered throughout reflects much credit to all concerned. Madam Porter sang the air " Pious orgies " very effec- tively, and at once won the sympathy of the audience by her clear enunciation and expression. Mr. Cuzuer threw very little fire into his first efforts during the evening, and his singing of "'Tis well, toy friends," was rather tame; but in the air, "Sound an alarm," he gave clear evidence of his power as a tenor singer, and was loudly applauded. ' Miss Davies sang with considerable sweetness as the "priest and the ruesseeger," and appeared to be a favourite with the audience. But the choruses were the great feature of the performance, and they appeared to increase in Swished excellence as the uralorio proceeded. "We come, we come, in bright array," "Disdainful of danger, we'll rush on the foe,' and "We never, never will bow down," were capitally given, but they "paled their in- effectual fires" before the One, "See, the conquering hero comes," which was magnificently sung. The proceedings concluded shortly after ten o'clock. div.head: 21ST L.R.Y. SHOOTING.
div.p: 21ST L.R.Y. SHOOTING.

The annual closing match of the above corps, for the season took place on Saturday, at Sutton range. It took the form of a triangular match, viz.—the St. Helens Com- panies (A, C, 11, and G,) v. the Sutton and Ravenhead Com- panies (B, E, and F,) v. the Widnes and Prescot Companies) H, I, and K), twelve men on each aide; ranges, 200 and 500 Yards; seven shots, with one sighter at each distance; Snider rifles; any position. The afternoon was tolerably fine, although it got rather dark before all the shooting was quite finished; wind moderate, but rather variable from rear to right rear. The St. Helens Companies' men, who had to sloaot with one or two members who happened to be on the ground, their full team not all turning up, were still the winners, with a good average of 54.25 points; the Sut- ton and Ravenbead Companies making an average of 52.83 points, and the Widnes and Prescot companies 51.16 points. The average for the whole 36 men was thus 52 74 points. Sergeant F. J. West's score of 66 out of a possible 70 is noteworthy, and was made up as follows :-200 yards: 445 5 5 5 5-33. 500 yards: 535 5 5 5 5-33. Also is that of Private Norbury, a young and rising shot, who mode 64. 200 yards : 55 4 4 4 5 5-32. 500 yards: 54 3 5 5 5 5 —32. A collision took place on the Silloth and Carlisle Railway yersterday, near Abbey Junction, between two goods traitor. One driver is seriously injured ; vans and trucks smashed, and traffic interrupted. 1 Thomas Butler, pointsmau, was brouht before the magjc. trates at Hinckley yesterday, charged with the mauslaughtto of the persona killed in the late Desford accident upon the Midland Railway. Prisoner was committed for trial. At Ballyfarnen, Roscommon, last night, a party of man attacked a coulees house, wrecked the furniture, severely illtreating the occupier, and made the man promise to leave his employment, his master having been Boycotted. The man refuses to identify the perpetrators. THE POACHING AFTRAT AT LYIIIM.-At the Alttincham Police Court, on Thursday, Thomas Willis, John Hitches'. and James Lenin, rock salt getters, were charged on remand with having been concerned in the poachilag affray on the , estate of Colonel Legh, of High Legh, near Lymm. on the 7th inst., when Joseph Jennings, one of the poachers. was killed. The prisoners were farther remanded.
STOI PING THE SALVATION ABIET.—AIa special meeting
of the Oxford magistrate; held yesterday, it was resolved

that the Salvation. Army procession should be no longer allowed, in consequence of their causing breaches of Om peace, and a notice was ordered to be issued stating that the Police have directions to prevent the formation of such pp- cessions, and to apprehend all persons found committing any breach of the law.

STAFFORD ELECTION .—The nomination took place yester- day. Thomas Salt ( C), gentleman, was nominated by Alderman John Averill, seconded by Councillor William Wright; also by W. G. Bagnall, seconded by John Kelsall, jun. George Howell (L), journalist, was proposed by Wm. Sylvester, seconded by George Keogh, manager of the Working Men's Club; also by Henry Elackmoore, seconded by J. T. Evans. The polling will take place to-day. The town is very quiet.

The friends of Lefroy are still busily engaged procuring ! proof as to the alleged insanity in prisoners family, at the same time not neglecting to petition for his reprieve. . An uncle, whose address was unknown, has come forward within the past few days, and has given much information affect. ing the question of insanity. A letter has this week been rec6ived by the convict's cousin, Mr. Seale, in which he re- fers to his past life and to his coming death, and speaks of the peace of mind which he now feels in looking forward to his end.

S ETADIEFIIL FLOGGING OF Gante.—The Glaßyow Daily Mail, yesterday, contained serious charges of mismanagement in the Glasgow Girls' Industrial School. They relate chiefly to shameful cases of flogging of the girls of that institution. One girl named Park was flogged (naked), and afterwa:rda Placed under a spray bath "to cool her down." The sub- committee of inquiry, by a majority, have decided that to confidence can be placed in the matron, and they recommend that her resignation be accepted, but the general committee have yet to come to their decision.

GREAT DIAMOND ROBBERY. One of the most daring Post Office robberies ever pi:mm(l in this country has taken place at Hatton-garden, London, which is a great diamond-cutting centre. On •Wednesday evening, while the officials at this branch office were busily employed making up the mails, the gas on the premises was suddenly turned off, and in the confusion which followed bags were abstracted containing the letters thht had been regtstead di irg the day.. The lett rs C,rliin valuable property estimated ta be wort:: as much as £40,000. The thief got safely of ol'h his boty, ar:dtm to the Preseht no clue ha e been obtaimd to his whereabouts. No doubt is entertained that the whole affair was !mat ski!fulty planned, and it is belitved that the audacious robber tua.t hove had nne accomplice who was familiar with the arram!aments of the office. The stolen property included a qua;)fiti, of jewellery and diamonds, and many of the letters, in addi ion to being registered, were insured.- The robbery was carried out with the most perfect ease, the thief simply taking the mail bags fi cm the nail on which they were hanging, and making his escape in the darkness. THV WIDNES KICKING CASE. ••

At the Liverpool Winter Assizes, yellsterdaY, before' Sir Edward Kay, Thomas Mitchell (19), Peter Haverty (21), and Timothy Mitchell (20), all labourers, who were found guilty of wounding David Plumptoc, at Widnes, on the Ist Octo- ber last, by kicking him, were brought up for sentence. His Lordship observed that the case was one which, to his mind, was entirely inexplicable.. He could not conceive what induced the prisoners to commit the very grievous offence of whiai they had been convicted. The prosecutor said "Good night be them as they passed, and he supposed Ithey thought the observation to be an insult. That was the only way in which he could imagine that they committed I this gross and abominable assault. There had been banded to him a number of letters stating that the prisoners were steady men, and nothing had been known against them before. He knew nothing of them, and was bound to treat their offences as lightly as he could, but it was abominable that men like the prisoners should attack a man who bad done them no harm, throw him on the ground, and in a brutal and cowardly manner kick him in the face. That was a crime which, he was sorry to say, was prevaltnt in these towns in the north, and therefore he was bound to visit it with a severe sentence in spite of allablaat had been said in their behalf. He could not distinguish between the criminality of each of them, and they would each be sentenced to fifteen months' imprisonment with hard labour.

div.p: SLAIN- BY DRINK AT RUNCORN.

Yesterday afternoon, Mr. Woreley, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Railway Hotel, on the body of John Bracegirdle, plater, of No. 19, Cavendish-street, Newtown who committed suicide by strangling himself with a rope The following evidence was given :—Nathaniel Bracegirdle slater, of :10, Sevell-street, said deceased was his uncle, and about 66 years of age. Deceased was rather given to drink, and for some years his wife had not lived with him. He bad not seen him for about a month. He did not know of any trouble which deceased had bad, with the exception of having heard a report to the effect that a summons had been sent from a neighbouring town to be served upon him for not maintaining his wife. He believed it was about 20 years since Bracegirdle separated from his wife.—Mr. James Kirk- ham, joiner and builder, Greenway-road, said he had em- ployed deceased for about twenty years, and last saw him alive on the previous Saturday. On Saturday week, he paid, him his ways, and told him that he must leave the amount of his eat flings to go ton-aids the nnt he ot d him for the house he occupied. hi the Tn.wday after g ~at storm Of wind, deceased commenc..l drinking, and Ii ii t,ot attended to his I,,bonr since, but itS bad a man and h w.,rking for , him. On VS'edn.tyby b,g, ft ~rn some repot:, •Ahich had I been in clrcicath,n, it tl s to break he house where &ceased d (-a :I.( 'rowing runrt g n doing I so, ttly saw dr,?-1(4.,/ tyl.l /or n his stomach, itl his bead against the wJ. ot b a rope round his mels id a slate,'s , " straight-eeg, " in his band. From the tat,- ment of the witness, it appeared that the deceased had strangled himself by the aid of the rope and the piece of wood on the bed, and tumbled on the floor of the house whilst doing so.—By the Coroner: Did he owe you anything? Yes, about £4 for rent.—Had you threatened him at all ? I gave him notice on the Monday. I also stopped the man and boy who worked under, him ; and said that if I could not get mv work from him, I must put a stop to his drinking. I tried to find him, but I could not do so; and on Monday morn- into I put the notice to quit the house under the doer. If I was busy at my place deceased would be sure to be drink- ing, and if matters were dull, be would always be hanging about the place and begging and praying for work. De- ceased was a very intemperate man. I have spoken to him far oftener than I should have done to my own brother, on which at timp he has said, "Say no more or I shall make myself away; lam ready to drown myself." I have never beard that he had suffered from traces of insanity.—The Coroner: I think that the facts are•very clear that this man seems to have drunk himself into a state of insanity.l He has just had wit enough to know how to hang himself, and that has hem about all.—Wm. Salkeld, a fish hawker, of Pennington's-row, to whom the Coroner paid the compli- merit that he had given his evidence remarkably well, said that for about nine years he was a reighbour to deceased. He last saw hint on Sunday morning, when he looked very wild, but was quite sober. He bad seen deceased on the Saturday, and he therefore asked him how he felt. He re- plied,"lain very bad; I am miserable and ready to put an end to my life. Everything is going badly against me; and I have a great deal of work on hand which I am letting get behind. I don't think I shall be fit for work on Monday." On other occasions he had told witness that he -had bad a deal of money to pay his wife, and was getting behindhattd with his contributions, which were at the rate of 4s. per week.—Thomas Peers, SO, Shaw-street, labourer, proved getting a ladder and entering the back bedroom of Bracegirdle's house, and finding the body upon the floor.—Alfred Ward, of No. 17, Cavendish-street, joiner, who lives next door to deceased's, said that on Mon- day.night he site hint at the bottom of Shaw-street. Deceased said he was in a very poor way; his bed had not been made for four days; the dishes had not been washed for a week; there was ' no poor devil as badly off as he was"; and be wished he was dead.—Sergeant McMichael gave evidence as to breaking into the deceased's house and finding the body, upon which there were no marks of vjolence.—The emu : I think there is no doubt that deceased has committed suicide .whllst labouring under his troubles. I think that this death is one more to be attri- bated to the fatal curse of drink. There is not the slightest doubt in my mind that this poor man, by his intemperate habits, got his affairs into such an inextricable mess, that he thought there was no way of getting out of them without destroying himself, and, acting under that misguided notion, he committed suicide.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased committed suicide whilst labouring under temporary insanity.—Mr. Robert Wright, one of the Jurymen, said that deceased would have to be buried at the expense of the town. •

div.head: BIGAMY AT ST. HELENS
div.p: BIGAMY AT ST. HELENS

Josebh Newton was yesterday morning, charged with marrying Esther Westhead at Liverpool whilst his former wife was alive. Newton was formerly manager of the Liberal Club, and lived with his wife until a few months ago when they separated. He was married at Lowe House Church, twenty years ago, on the seventh October. lie married Westhead. He was apprehended on Thursday night in Lyon-street.—Prisoner pleaded guilty and was committed to the assizes.—Bail was accepted. •

HOQPITAL SUNDAY.—Following the custom which has been established in St. Helens, of adopting the Sunday following the election of May& as " Hospital Sunday," simultaneous sermons were preened, and collections made on Sunday last id the churches and chapels of the town, on behalf of the Cottage Hospital. The Mayor (Mr. R. Pilk- iugton) carried out his intention of attending the Congrega- tional Chapel on Sunday with his accustomed privacy. There was a large congregation. In the course of the service, the Rev. R. J. Ward made the Mayor, the Cottage Hospital, and the British and Foreign Bible Society the subject of special prayer, and also referred to them in appropriate terms in the course of his sermon. The rev. gentleman took for his text Romans xiv. 7,8, 9., " For none of us lived] to himself, and none dieth to himself. For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; or whether we die, we die unto the Lord : whether we live therefore or die, we are the Lord's. For to this end Christ died, and lived again, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living." He delivered an eloquent and able discourse, which was listened to with marked attention.

div.p: the courage of my convictions, and will dare to do what is right. To-morrow I may be found denouncing the conduct of an employer as strongly as I condemn yours to-day.— Yours re JAMES CAPPER, Operatives Secretary. Stafford-street, Walsall, November 12th, 1881. Mr. John Chalmers. Sir,—Will you allow us a short space in your valuable paper to offer a i few remarks upon particular statement in the letter which appeared n your issue on the 12th inst. signed " Paddle?" Upon the general features of that letter we do not now concern ourselves, but in the list of changes the writer enumerates, siad to have been effected by Mr. Mc nearly the last, but not least, is that Mr. Morris proposed a scheme instead of the Employers' Liability Act which was to be all the men could desire, but it so moulded that I shall be surprised if any sensible man agrees to it. the Now, caseovr,s sir, t permit say themitu least o s letosayf it th, at the way " Paddle " puts misleading, and calcu- lated to create a false impression in the public mind, and has already nicle the impression that Mr. Morris moulded the scheme himself, and that the men had simply to bear, endorse, and ratify what he suggested. Such was not the case. rh ere was a sub-committee from the general committee for that important work, and Mr. Morris had no more to do with drawing up the code of rules we have passed than any other member of the committee, more than from the fact that he may possess a keener intellect and riper judgment than perhaps some who were on the commit- tee. But sir, we are proud to say there were men on that committee who have not shunned to express themselves in opposition to Mr. Morris's suggestions, and argued their points with such intelligent clearness and sustained them with such cogency of argument as to carry the committee with them in many cases, and when the various points have been thoroughly discussed we are frank to say they were honourably put to the meeting and the majority ruled, in some cases in direct opposition to Mr. Morris's suggestions. It will thus be seen that the scheme has not been moulded for the men, but by the men, which is a very important dis- tinction, which I hope " Paddle " will observe. We have made the very best case we possibly could, and we are not ashamed of our work, from the simple fact that we defy " Paddle" to point out a single instance throughout the country where they have done better. We should like to refer "Paddle " to a letter in which the owners of Podmore Hall Colliery, Newcastle-under-Lyme, disclaimed any wish in any way to influence their men with regard. to the Em- ployers' Liability Act, but it was put to the men that it boa serious matter if upon every accident occurring a law suit should ensue. Mr. Craig, M.P., one of the proprietors, had stated in the House of Commons that in his opinion the proper course to adopt was to join in mutual insurance, and a fair and reasonable contribution from employers would be 50 per cent. It was urged that this is' not contracting out of the Act, but in accordance with the terms of the Act. In the Podmore Hall case it secures the unfortunates 9s. per week instead of Cs. In our case it secures the unfortunates 15s. per week instead 10s., so that we say we are not ashamed of our work. But sir, it is not so much to plead for the mutual principle that we write as to remind 'Paddle" of the personal insult he has off red to every member of our committee. He has offered an insult to our honour, intelli- gence, and manliness. We must remind "Paddle" if he had attended only one of our committee meetings he would have seen at once we were not so many dummies without brain or thought as to sit there and simply hear and endorse every- thing that was suggested, but that there was a free inter- change of opinion, and the plucky, determined manner in which the different members pressed their points proved at once that more minds than one were at work. Then " Paddle " said it was "to be all men could desire." Nothing in the whole range of human life comes up to that point, for it is a trite saying, "There is a fly in every pot of oint- ment," but we Fay it is all we could reasonably expect. Then as to his last remark, "I should be surprised if any sensible man agrees to it." Now, sir, there are different ways of looking at things. In our judgment all sensible rivm will agree to it, and if we did not think in our hearts it would he a mutual benefit for our fellow workmen we cer- tainly should never have countenanced it from the first. We have officially, as secretaries, examined into all the cases of accident this year, and they have not been few, and we say that proceedings under the Act could not have been taken in one single case. If all the unfortunates had taken " Paddle's " advice they would not have reined the benefit of the extra ss. per week, as they have done. Would that have been a sensible proceeding? According to " Paddle " it would. But we venture to say that the unpr-judiced reader will say no. Hoping " Paddle" will give us credit for honesty when we say we are acting for the general goad, and as we are a common brotherhood we need a few " help- one-another-societies," which we think would be a good name for ours. Apologising for the length of our letter, wa remain, yours, Dallam Forge, I. J. BIDDLE, Secs. Warrington, Nov. 16, 1881. L. WEIR,
;rriS,

under the roof while you were there. It would not have taken a minute? Witness: Well, you can't exactly make a man do it in it moment. —The Coroner: Oh, yes you can. You did not think it was necessary lam afraid.—Mr. Hall: When you visited the deceased did it not strike you that he had been working in great danger for some con- siderable time through not having props under the roof? Witness: No. The top coal was knocked, and it seemed solid enough. lie ordered the deceased to take the top coal down, but he did not obey it seemed.—Mr. Hall said he had inspected the place. There could not be a doubt that the top coal should have been timbered; and if not timbered, it ought to have been cut down. But if, the manager told the deceased what be, said he did, he was pretty well satisfied they bad done what they could.—The Coronet: Would it not have been much wiser on the part of the manager if he bad made deceased put a prop down while he was there? Mr. Hall: Yes; it would have been much wiser.—The Coroner observed that the death of the poor fellow had oc- curred through his own mistake.—The Foreman thought there should be a strong recommendation to the officials that the men employed on similar work should prop their places or cease work at ence.—The Coroner said they had the Act of Parliament. The master could not stand by the man till he had done his duty. He could give the order, and if it was neglected he could order the man out of the pit.—A juryman remarked that deceased was especially a careful man, and must have had very great confidence in the stability of the roof. He had known deceased to play many a day when he thought there was any danger in the pits.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

WARRINGTON PARLIA.MENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. The attendance at the weekly meeting of the House on Monday evening was more satisfactory than it has been for some, time past. On the Ministerial side the muster of members was an average one, but the attendance of the Opposition has not been equalled since the opening of the session. Instead of the dozen gentlemen who week after week have represented the Conservatives with unfailing regularity, the members of the Opposition came up in strong force, and when the Speaker (Dr. Huson-More) took the chair about eight -o'clock, tbe House assumed the crowded appearance so often noticeable during the late session. As the evening progressed the number of Conservatives waft greatly augmented by the arrival of hon. members who have seldom been present at debates, but who doubtless felt it incumbent to respond to the " whip " which had been issued in the expectation of a division on the oaths' question. The attendance of strangers, too, large as it was at the previous sitting, was greatly exceeded on this occasion, several ladies being amongst the visitors whose interest in the proceedings had in no way abated. The adjourned debate of the motion for the abolition of the Parliamentary • oath was resumed by the Secretary for the Colonies, who re- marked that there were many things which were popular in this latter half of the nineteenth century which might be strictly regarded as belonging to the childhood of the world and he regarded this oath question as a relic or old world superstition. It was a fact, he stated, that no matter what the pledge there was always a number of people who would break it, and he declared they no more regarded the taking of an oath than they did the swallowing of a pint of beer. The right hon. mem- ber who introduced the-motion believed we had arrived ate period of the world's history when men should regard themselves as men, and not as children. He said he was sorry the Leader of the Opposition was not present, and created con:iderable amusement by reading a short poem

relative to the action of the right -hon. member for West Cheshire at the last sitting of the house. Proceeding to criticise the speech of the right hon. member for Truro, be adverted to the statement that the question involved a change in the constitution, and denied the correctness of the statement, inasmuch as the highest legal authorities declared to the contrary. As to the statement that these were ceremonies, he remarked they pleased parsons, grown-UP children, and women. The people of this country, if appealed to on a question of this sort, would, he declared, decide it in a broader and more comprehensive sense than the right hon. gentleman had any idea of. It was part oat the unwritten constitution of this country to protest not only against certain forms but forms of bigotry and intoler- ance from wheiesoever they might come; and the people would, if appealed to, protest against any further imposition ,of the oath upon those who objected to it. As to the question being decided by the electors of Northampton, he said it bad been decided by those who had elected Mr. Bradlaugh as their member, and it was only bigotry and intolerance, the offspring of.. ignorance, that prevented him taking his seat. The experience of this country knew enough of what liberty was under Roman Catholicism, but we had not had the experience of Atheism in any country. , fie expressed his belief that the administration of the oath , j was the gate hypocrisy and concluded by supporting the motion.—While he could not commend either the language used or the manner in which the Secretary for India Introduced the subject, the member for Newcastle- on-Tyne was compelled to express his sympathy vith the right hon. gentleman in the peculiar circumstances . . . .

THE 'RELIGIOUS CENSUS. filir,—We should be glad if you will kindly insert the :knowing in your neat issue. I find you have been misin- Alarmed respecting the Workingmen's Mission Sabbath Adobocat Baal; Q,`1437. The report says that there was only a WWI school in the afternoon, when the fact was quite the asverse, as every class was, and has been now for some time, ,cary much overcrowded, the numbers present, including facers and teachers, being over 300.—Your obedient servant, FRANCIS WILLIA.MS, Secretary. Virarrington. Sir,—Tne religious census which you published last week AshoWs a most deplorable state of affairs as regards the aroligions life of this country. I hope that those who are terested in the religious institutions of the country syill Death* themselves, and see whether something cannot be done to remedy it. We. hear so much about Christianity in this our eulightened country—which is often called a Christian land—that we are sometimes inclined to think if all We hear is true that the great majority of the people are Christians. But the statistics which you published last Week show that the great masses of the people attend no place of worship whatever, and instead of raising so much stir about sending missieoaries oat to heathen countries, an intelligent foreigner, placed in possession of these facts, Would say " Evangelise your own countrymen at your own /JONATHAN. 'doom first."—Yours truly, THE PEDDLERS' STRIKE AT WARRINGTON. r , —Will you allow roe, throngh the medium of your columns, CO say a few words in reference to a letter in 7he Examiner of the sth last, signed "With the men." The district named by him is Lancashire; and be knows as Well as Ido that the prices paid for puddling, with the exception of one or two works, is better than the men received at Bewsty for the class of iron they work. He mentions a works or two, but does not say what kind of I happen to know, from per- iron they are working. Now, sorted knowledge the parts be refers to. At Maybury isnd Marsden's, they work the ctromonest of iron and mine fettling, for which they receive is 3 ; but sorely he does not mean to put the Bewsey men on a footing with them, when their iron is far superior than theirs. He then mentions Barningham's works. The men there—and you must know, I speak from personal knowledge—work com- mon bars for 73 9d per ton and scraps at is 9d also. while at Bewsey they ground b irs at 75 61 per ton, and the men at this works work all pastes' fettling mine, blue billy, and red ore, all grand together, and no cinder fettling what- ever do they work; and the paste:, fettling worked by this Works is a fettiing far superior to that which the masters of Bewsey forge want their men to work. Why does he not give some instances of the leading works in Lancashire, so that the public might judge for themselves? this he omits. lie only takes those works which suit h s purpose. This, sir, shows his case to be very weak, from his point; and I would have hint to be honest in his quotations when he again writes for the benefit of the public. Again, he says nothing about a works he must have passed when at these works he mentions, where the men a few months ago worked their common iron at is 31 and scraps at 55 9.1. now working the same iron at is 9.1 and scraps at is 31 per ton; nor of other firms close by, which be must know are working their iron I at a price above Bewsey for the quality they work; and the firms he refers to at Sheffield work their wire iron at Bs, 93 6d, and lOs 61 per ton; and all mine fettling. So, air, with this before the public, they will be able to judge for themselves if " With the men " is right or wrong in his remarks.—Yours, BAR, ENDS.

Sir,—ln pursuing the columns of last Saturday's issue I observd a letter signed " Paddle." charging Mr. Morris with Moulding a scheme of insurance, and saying be would be surprised "if any sensible man agreed to it." Now, had "Paddle" (before loosing his canoe off) made the necessary enquiries before inserting the insinuation, he would have been informed that the committee chosen by the men had the full power (and not Mr Morris) of compiling and pass- ing all laws for the guidance of the society, and they are such as the committee feel confident will meet with the general approval of all sensible men I can truthfully state , that Mr. Morris has done all that lies in his power to secure as much benefit for the members as the funds would possibly allow, both in the case of accidents, and the clause referring to deceased members' families. Now, sir, I tldnk " Paddle ". has not carefully considered matters before taking Up his pen, or I think he would have felt the depth of the stream before launching his bark. Apologising for trespassing on your valuable space.—Yours, A COMMITTEE MAN. _

Sir,--In your issue of Saturday last there appeared. I will not say a letter, but a confused m las of misstatements re- specting the Bowser poddlers' dispute, signed by "Paddle." Naw, while I have a wholesome dislike to have any deal- ings with persons who find it convenient to take shelter behind the anonymous, there is one statement made by "Pachile"respecting myself, which, with your kind permission I must claim to brie-fly notice. "[Wale" states that the Bewsey puddlers did not ask for my advice or interference. "Paddle" is either ignorant of facts, or his statement is deliberately false, as I have in my p msession several letters addressed ta me by Mr. John Chalmers, who has been pre- siding ever the meetings of the men on strike, asking me for information and advice, which I have given in a truthful and nanAid manner. In support of my position, I will, with Mr. John Chalmers' permission, make the contents of his letter public.; then your readers will be able to judge the value of "Paddle's" statement. I never interfere between masters and men unless requested to do so, and not even then except by virtue of my official position. Herewith I enclose copy of my last letter addressed to Mr. John Chalmers. Kindly pub- lish it in connection with this in your next issue. It will the more clearly explain the little part that I have taken in the Bewsay paddlers' dispute. While I thank the Warrington iron- workers for their exceeding kindness to me in the past, I will never stoop to defend them in doing that which I believe to be wrong. Thanking you in anticipation for your fovour, I am, dear sir, yours most respectfully JAMES CAPPER, Operatives Secretary. South eaffordslaire Mill and Forge Wages Board. Stafford-street, Walsall, November 14th,1881.

Dear sir, -- In yours of 9th instant, you advise me that you are instructed by the Strike Committee to say that they can dispense with my services in the present dis- pute, as the men on strike are not members of the board that I represent. yet in the next paragraph of your letter you state that the Strike Committee wish we to supply them with certain letters—which, I must remind you, are the private prop ,cty of the Board with which you admit you Trave no connection. In pursuing such tactics as these, your Striking Committee cannot boast of being consistent, and, on reflection, they must conclude that they could not reasonably expect to be further served by the person whose services they have dispensed with. You and your striking friends may console yourselves that it will not give me pain, but, on the other hand, if will afford me at least some little relief to be dismissed from a position which I did seek, and had no desire to occupy, and from serving men who, it is clear, are not prepared to listen to either common sense or reason. Had you, and those who are now acting with you, been reasonable men you would not have taken offence be- cause the information and advice which you asked for was not what you wished for. You and your friends should remember that it was not me who created the conditions of of labour existing in the puddling departments of the other works in and outside of Warrington. I only fairly repre- sented to you such conditions as I found them to exist, as it becomes my duty to do, and as any honourable man ; placed in my position would feel himself bound to do. The ' alvice which I offered to you and your friends when asked for it was offered by me with the best and purest of motives, and.you and your friends have committed a most grievout mistake in not accepting it and acting upon it in the same spirit which prompted me to give it. I told you in plain and respectful terms that the little matter in dispute between . yen and your employers was a case for reference, and I Logged of you in almost pleading tones to try and keep clear of a strike, and to agree with your employers to submit the case to arbitration. This you and your friends have refused to do, and your refusal I make bolt to say is prima facie evidence, that you have a bad case, and hence you are afraid to submit it to the test of intelligent and honest investigation. Hitherto I have abstained from saying a single word upon the merits of the case in dispute, but as you and your friends have refused to act in a spirit of conciliation, and are now opmly fighting against the principle of arbitration, I deem it only right that I should do so. The employers and the employed in St iffordshire, and the employers and the employed in the north of England have been brought nearer to each other by the influence of social intercourse, and they are begin- ning to learn that each other's motives are not so bad as they appear to be when looked at from a distance through the distorting atmosphere of industrial conflict. Now you and your friends have not much to complain of on the score of treatment received from Pearson, Knowles, and Co., and their management in the past. You have been most f or- tunattly situated, and during the past seven years of nn- paralel al trade depression, you have had the benefit of more raguiar mployroent together with a little higher wage than the purl., -rs in other districts. Your present action reminds me of ti title of one of Shakespeare's plays, namely, " Much a ) about nothing." Your case is confined to a nutshell, a lie explained and made clear in a very few words. It ,tands thus :—At Monks, Hall, and Co.'s, the neighbourinl: works, the pudelers are supplied with all mine for fettling purposes, and they are paid 7s. 9d. per on for puddling common wire iron. At Dallam, Forge, which i 3 one of the forges belonging to Pearson, Knowles, and Co., the puddlers are also supplied with all mine and iron and are paid 7s. 9d. per ton for puddling common wire and hoop iron. The 11-xsey Forge puddlers were supplied with part mine and vie calcined cinder, and were paid Ss. per ton for puddling same classes of iron, the 3d. extra being allowed for usi: is one part calcined cinder. Now the only alteration a.: 'i the management claim the right to make is to cease the .upply of the calcined cinder, and in turn the puddlers arc simply asked to waive their claim to the 3d. extra, on the ground that they are not now required to use it. If an appeal were to be made to the puddlers employed at any other forge apart from Bewsey, and they were asked which they would prefer, all mine with 78. 9d. per ton, or part mine and part calcined cinder with Ss. per ton, they would most assuredly pronounce in favour ofth e former conditions. All mine, as compared witb calcined I cinder, tends to lesson the puddler's labour, and at the same time tends to produce a larger output of iron. Therefore. when using ,!hab tohui all mine, instead of part mine and part ,calcined cinder, there would be a decrease in the without any decrease in his wages. By yPwudridtlienrga style you and your friends may conclude that I have i sympathy with the party now en strike, and n this you would be quite correct, but you must remember that I have.
