div.head: THE. EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 19, 1881. RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: THE. EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 19, 1881. RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

The Rev. J. NOWELL moved a resolution giving the hearty thanks of the meeting to the committee and. collectors, and appointing the committee for the ensuing year; which was seconded by Mr. THOMAS NOIIMAN, and carried unani- mously.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. S. B. Chadwick chairman), and Charles Reynolds. SINGULAR CHARGE AGAINST A BEERHOTJSE KEEPER.— Mrs. Sarah Abrams, landlady of the Blue Ball, beerhouse, Fryer-street, was summoned on three charges, the first being for selling intoxicating liquor at a quarter past two on the morning of the 9th instant; the second for selling the liquor during prohibited hours ; and the third for refusing to admit Sergeant Walley and Constahle Noden to the house.—Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the defence.—Superintendent Williamson said that about a quarter past two on the morn- ing in question, the two officers were on duty in the vicinity of the defendant's house. They heard a noise caused by the rattling of jugs and glasses in the vaults, and remained to listen. They concealed themselves in a passage, and after waiting a short time, they saw Samuel Massey and Martin Dunn come out of the IP,use. Massey carried a half gallon bottle, wrapped up in a handkerchief. On being questioned, he admitted the bottle contained beer. The men said that the liquor had been drawn before eleven o'clock at night. The officers then went to defendant's house, where they saw a light. They called out "police," and knocked at the door a great number of times, but no answer was returned for about twenty-five minutes. Mrs. Abrahams told the officers that the beer had been drawn before eleven o'clock. Sergeant Walley and P.C. Noden were called and gave ea i- deuce to this effect.—Mr. Linaker said his client admitted the facts stated on behalf of the prosecution, as they had been very fairly and honestly stated by Sergeant Walley, who always gave his evidence in that court with remarkable fairness. The defendant for naany years had full charge of the Bull's Head publichouse, which was formerly kept by her husband, who was a sailor, and during all that time there was never a report made against her. Massey had been a waiter in the house for some time ; and during the day his wife had asked the landlady and a lodger named Dunn, to ' go to her house to supper, as it was her birthday. About half-past nine Mrs. Abrams said she could not go as she was not very well, but they might have sapper at her own house after closing time. Previous to this the beer had been put in a battle for the purpose of being taken to Mrs. Massey's. They remained at supper until about two o'clock in the morning, and then went home. On their way Massey and Dunn agreed to teturn and fetch the bottle of beer. On leaving the house a second time, they were met by the two policemen.— The defendant, Massey, Samuel Dunn, and Mary Parr were called for the defence.—The Chairman said the case was cer- tainly a suspicious one, and one which the police were per- fectly justified in bringing before them, but after the ex- planation which had been given, the summonses would be dismissed.—,The Superintendent of Police said he would with- draw two other summonses, in which Dunn and Massey were charged with having been on the premises during prohibited hours. POOR RATES FOR HALTO2.I.—ThS magistrates sanctioned a new poor's rate for Halton, at Bd. in the L. DRUNIIENNE,S.—John Howard, who had been previously convicted several times, was fined 20s. and 9s, 60. costs, or, in default of payment, one month's imprisonment. A Row IN REGENT-STREET.—William Hignett, a coloured man, was summoned for having used defamatory language towards a respectably dressed woman named Mary Leach.— Complainant said as she was going up her entry at about ten o'clock on the sth instant, defendant called her an immoral Irishwoman, and mentioned a man named PI itchard as one with whom she WAS too familiar.—William Pritchard and Catherine Pritchard were called to support the complainant's statement.—Defendant was also charged rvith assaulting William Pritchard, a witness in the other case, who lives in Regent-street.—Mr. Barton appeared for the complainant.— Complainant said on the night of the sth inst., he took home s;xpennyworth of fireworks, and let them off in his yard. Defendant called over the wall on which he asked him what he wanted._ .Hignett said he would "let him know what he

wanted," if he did not make a less-noi-s-e-. --H-O:t-hen. enquired of Hignett if be was a boy that he was so irritated at so little a thing. Defendant then struck him on the breast, on which he hit him, but seeing that he was under the influence of drink, he picked him up. Defendant then struck him on the breast, seized him by the hair, and kicked him on the sides, the legs, and the stomach.—Mrs. Leach gave corro- borative evidence. Pritchard was next charged with assault- ing Hignett on the same night. Complainant said he was going down the entry when defendant fired what he believed was a pistol, which frightened him very much. He was so annoyed that he shouted out "You old thickhead; you want your head knocking off." Defendant then knocked him down, and got upon him. He was pulled off by a man Jack Hedley. He and defendant afterwards had further altercation, but though the wall was between them, Pritchard managed to hit him on the head with a chair. The blow was so severe that it cut his head severely, and he lost much blood.—A woman named Mrs. Abrams said she heard the pistol discharged, and was very much alarmed with it.—P.C. Noden gave evidence as to the complainant going to the police office and showing his wounds. The magistrates ordered Pritchard to enter into sureties to keep the peace, himself in £lO and onein £5 to keep the peace for six months. The charge of assault against Hignett was dismissed ; but he was ordered to enter into sureties, himself in £lO and one in £5, for six months, for using the defamatory language. THE WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT.—George Mort, shop- keeper, Rutland-street, was summoned for having in his possession a pair of scales which were unjust.—Superinten- dent Williamson, the inspector under the Act, said he visited _ . . . _

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

WmarcEsnay.—Before Mr. H. S. Hall. The principal cases were adjourned, owing to the fact that a second magistrate was unable to attend, as nearly all the justices were engaged at Liverpool assizes. TRESPASSING ON THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN LINE.—John Small and George 'Rogerson, two respectably dressed men, were summoned for offending against the Lon- don and North - Western bye- laws by trespassing on the line near a level crossing.—Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitors' department, Lime-street, Liverpool, appeared on behalf of the company, and said that the bye-law under which the defendants was summoned had beeu passed for the protection of individuals and the line itself. The bye- law provided that any person trespassing upon any level crossing, after having been once warned, should be liable to a penalty not exceeding 40s. The crossing was one near the Widnes foundry. [lt will be remembered that some time ago two men were killed at this crossing, and that the coroner made some very strong remarks as to the railway com- pany not being strict enough in summoning offenders.] An official of the company said that a few minutes after twelve o'clock on the 18th October, he cautioned the two defect- dents about trespassing on the line near the crossing; but on the Bth inst., he found them upon it again.—Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, remarked that he believed only a very short time had elapsed since the company put a man at the Place named in order to deal with trespassers.— Mr. Hall observed that, under the circumstances, it might meet the requirements of the law if he inflicted merely a nominal penalty.—Mr. Ferrand replied that the company had no wish to press the case unduly.—Defendants were each fined 2s. 61, and 7s. 6d. costs. ALLEGED THEFT By A LODGER—Patrick McDermott, a middle aged man, was charged, on remand, with stealing a silver watch and 15s. in money, the property of Joseph millo.—Prosecutor's wife said that up to thh previous Saturday prisoner had lodged with her at her house in 10xford-street. On Saturday afternoon, about four o'clock, he left saying that he should not return, and subseuently a black leather satchel, which contained an old silver watch and 15s. in money, was missed. The articles had been kept in a box, which was found broken open. Prisoner now said that the prosecutrix had been drinking with him on the day when he left the house, but this she denied, though she ad- mitted that her husband had.—The Inspector of Police said that the prisoner was traced to Runcorn, but none of the things were found upon him on his being apprehended.— The prisoner was remanded. BITTER WORDS BETWEEN TWO FARMERS. Mr. William Glace, a very extensive farmer at Upton, was summoned by Mr. Joseph Turton, a farmer at the same place, for using defamatory language towards him—Mr. Swift, junr., appeared for compldnant ; and Mr. Percy Davies, of Warrington, for the defence. The case excited considerable interest. Mr. Swift said that some six months ago, complainant had to summon the defendant for an assault committed upon him in Liverpool, for which he was fined Ll. A fortnight ago, at the Widnes court, Mr. Grace was summoned by the police, and, in making their enquiries, they asked complainant several questions. After the case had been disposed of, the parties happened to meet at Mr. Gerrard's public-house. Complainant was there when de- fendant came in, and, without any provocation, said" Heres goosey Turton. You killed your father, and robbed him of £3110; and you have caused your uncle Abram to hang himself." Ile need scarcely tell the court that there was no • - -lade by defendant ; . .

foundation whatever for tie charges Ifl, and if they had not been said in a manner which was highly calculated to cause a breach of the peace, the complainant could have afforded to have taken no notice of them— Complainant was called to support this statement.—ln cross- examination, witness said on the 26th ultimo, after leaving that court, he went to the Ball Inn, at Ditton, but he did not there make an observation to the effect that Mr. Grace was "bard up."—During the course of the cross-examination, Mr. Swift described one of the remarks of Mr. Davies as nirs mse, on which that gentleman, addressing Mr. Swift, observed, very warmly, "I beg your pardon, my cross- examinatian is not nonsense.—Mr. Swift: You have no right to ask the witness whether he is the sort of man to do such things.—M,. Davies : Then lam very sarry that you have not had sufficient experience to know that my question is a proper ene.—Witness further said that he had never said he would aggravate Mr. Grace, and he never gave him the slightest provocation .—Mr. Richard Wright, provision dealer, 51, Waterloo-road, Widnes, said he was in the public-house at the time of the alleged offence, and heard defendant make the remarks detailed by Mr. Swift. Mr. Porton got into a corner as if he were trying to get out of the way of Mr. Grace. He was in the house about fifteen minutes, and he never heard a word spoken by Mr Turton.—ln cross-examination, Mr. Davies asked the witness whereabouta he was sitting in the house at the time omneawshuricehmehnetrs when I am no n go into a —Joseph Moss, joiner, and Richard Baxter, 'Widnes, gave corroborative evidence. div.head: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS.
div.p: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS.

RUNCORN BRANCH. The services in connection with these missions commenced on Sunday, when the Rev. John Kilner, one of the general secretaries, and formerly missionary in Ceylon, preached twice in St. Paul's Chapel to large audiences. In the after- noon the various Sunday schools assembled in the same place of worship to hear an address from the Rev. Peter Hargreaves, returned missionary from South Africa, but as he had met with a slight accident, he was unable to be present, and his place was taken by the Rev. J. H. Cummings, of Widnes, who was at-one time missionary in India. On Monday evening the annual missionary meeting was held in the chapel, which was better filled than on any similar occasion for some years past. Mr. Joseph Cook, St. Helens presided, and there were also present, the Revs. John Nowell' (superintendent), George Hack, and John Kilner and George Hargreaves (the deputation); Messrs. John Simpson, Thomas Norman, J. R. Frith, C. Soulby, and Timothy Sitnister (secretary). The Rev. JOHN NOWELL briefly opened the proceedings, after which the CHAIRMAN called upon the secretary to read the report. Mr. SnetsrEn said his statement that evening would ooly deal with the local finances. The following amounts had been received from the Runcorn branch during the year St. Paul's Chapel, collected by Mrs. G. S. Hazlehurst, ID 195.; by Mrs. Simister, £7 145.; by Mrs. Soulby and Miss Harrison, £lO 12s. ;by Miss Peacock and Miss I Norman, £6 is. 6d.; public collection, £l4 15s. Id.; public I meeting, November 14th, £34 Bs. 81d. Public collection ire I Camden school chapel, Us. Halton-road :—Collected by Mrs. Frith, £4 58. Mill-brow Sunday school, £3 165.; public collections, £2 14s. 10d.; juvenile Christmas offerings, £9 4s. 7d. Brunswick Sunday school, collected in girls' classes, £3 14s. 4d.; in boys' classes, £9 Os. 3d.; by the boys, £ll Sc. 6,1.; by the girls with boxes £5 lie. ;by the girls with boxes, £29 35. 7d.; by the boxes, £9 19s. Iby the girls, £4 is. BA-d.; outside the school by the boys, £2 is. 3!-Ad.; by the girls outside the school, £8 Bs. lid.; and public collections, November 13, £1 17s. The total sum raised was £157 19s. 7d., being an increase of £l2 G. 6d. Of the total sum £l3 4s. sd. would be devoted to home missionary work. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said he was pleased to linci.that they took such a deep interest in missionary work in Runcorn. He was very sure that they could not do anything nobler than give their money for the purpose of sending the Gospel to those who could not pro- vide themselves with teachers of it. There were two or three items in the general report of the parent society, the perusal of which had encouraged him very much indeed, and he was convinced that they only needed to be laid before the meet- ing to commend themselves to their notice. The first matter to which he desired to refer was the spiritual work which was being carried on by their missionaries cn the Geld Coast, where " the work was being consolidated and extended." One of the members stated at the district meet- ing that he had seen the number of members there increase from 700 to 6,000. (Loud applause.) Surely they would be sufferers in their own souls if they did not give such a work all the support in their power. He was very desirous that the friends at Runcorn and other places should read the reports of the parent society for themselves. He was afraid that they were too often ignored, and the consequence was that their zeal for the missionary cause at times did not burn with so bright a flame as it would otherwise do. (Hear, hear.) The total amount of the home receipts by their society was £117,410, and towards this sum they had received from the foreign stations the handsome amount of £10,162. (Hear, hear, and .applause.) On the foreign stations, in addition to £110,074 for the purpose

this contribution, they had raised of carrying on the mission schools and for building pur- poses. (Applause.) Take Jamaica, which received a grant of £4,7o6—though a part of that was contributed by the societies in the island—where they had raised £lB,BOB for mission purposes, building schools, and carrying on the requirements of the mission. At Grahamstown the mission had received £4,556, and raised for similar purposes to those already stated. £11,842. (Loud applause.) The Rev. GEORGE HARGREAVES, who was received with applause, said he had bees much surprised at the remarks respecting returned missionaries. In fact he mhaadiehabdy spoenoipelde ifficulty in convincing many people that he was a returned missionary. Some had said that they could not believe that he was such, and had been in Africa twenty years. because he was not black. (Laughter.) Others of his friends said they could not believe that he had lived in the climate of Africa ; and when he asked them why ? They said it was because he was not thin. (Laughter.) But when he told them he had married an Aflicander curiosity was further raised, and they wanted to know whether she was black, and put all sorts of questions. It was in 1857 that he offered himself for the great work, and on Easter 'Monday, 1858, he reached his first and only circuit in Africa WARRINGTON ORM-TESTI-UT, —Clarkbury. For 24 years he had laboured and suffered there until the resurrection of the just. "Only a Rose" (Boyton Smith) and "The Three Fishers" (Hullah) were sung by her with a thorough earnestness which at once won sympathy. In regard to the last mentioned especially, we must own to discovering a new pathos in Miss Chatterton's rendering of this song. one, though simple, by no means easy to interpret truthfully. "No Sir," a humourous vocal nwrceau, given in response to a re-demand, was sung by Miss Chatterton with charming naivette, and won loud applause, The Kerry Dance' was scarcely so satisfactory a performance. To our mind the allusions in this song to pleasant memories, do not call for the display of such ecstatic feeling as that sourcht to be thrown into it by Miss Chatterton. He had only a letter from him last week asking for £lO, and he wrote at once back saying "Let him have what he wants from the grant." lie wanted £lO for the native school. They had to be very careful as missioneries, not to take a political side, but there might come a time when he should feel in a posi- tion to say something about the way in which South Africa was governed. The continent would never be made peaceful by setting one chief against the other, like the two Kilkenny cats ; and he was firmly convinced that if they could only get John Dunn and the other chiefs converted to God, there would be an end to the disputes. Witness said to him, " Dick, I am surprised at thee working in this way, and he replied," Well, Jim, I knocked at and it seemed solid." There were no props set. Had one been set it might have saved his life. When witness was engaged in similar work he either cut the top coal down or put a prop under it. When it was not loose, however, it was a job to get it down.—Mr. Hall Is it not a fact that in starting a place out of any old place there is a danger of "breaks " in the top coal, called "level cracks ?" Witness I have not seen any yonder.—l. Hall : But your experi- ence as a collier. Is there P- a danger of "breaks " or " settlements ? ' Witness t Yes, sometimes.—Mr. Hall: And would you not consider it more important to set timber when you were starting a place than afterwards? Witness : Yes, sir. PRESCOT WESLEYAN 711ITTTJAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. --The second lecture of the season in connection with this society was delivered on Wednesday, in the school-room, Chapel-street, by the Rev. B. W. Starr, of Liverpool, his subject being "A growl from John Bull, or the good old times." Mr. John Johnson Brown presided, and there was a moderate attendance. The Chairman, in opening the pro- ceedings, said a great deal of good, he thought, wouldsbe received on all sides if there was a little more fraternising between the different denominations existing in the town. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Starr reviewed at length the history of country from an early date down to the present time, and described in a lucid and glowing language the dress, manners, and customs of the people, the means of travelling, src. On the motion of the Chairman, a vote of thanks was • unanimously accorded to the lecturer, and a similar compli- ment having been paid the Chairman, the meeting separated. SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS JUNCTION. A shocking accident occurred on Wednesday morning, tit the St. Helena.junction of the London and Nortb-Western Railway, whereby a Roman Catholic priest, Fas%er Sebas- tian, of the Sutton Monastery, lost his life. It appears that the 9-30 am, train from Manchester to Liverpool was rather late, and arrived at the inflation about twenty minutes past ten, just as the ten o'clock express from Li,serpool to Man- chester was due. Deceased hurried on to the platform. asked i the train on the opposite side was for Liverpool, and t hen, though told to stand back, he stepped just in front o the express, and was knocked down and literally eut to pieces. His remains, which presented a shlrang spectacle, were removed to tbe Commercial Hotel. Deceased's ha, became entangled in the machinery underneath the engins, and was carried to Manchester. Father Sebastian was apparently about fifty years of age, and an Italian by birth For many years he resided in France, but about 12 month, ago was, along with other members of religious orders, ex- pelled from that country. Accordingly became to England and took up his quarters at Highgate London. Only thre. months ago he joined the priests at Sutton Monastery, St Helens, but, it is stated contemplated removing very shortly

IN PARLIAMENT.--SESSION 1882. SAINT HELENS (CORPORATION) WATER. (Construction of Waterworks—Compulsory Purchase of '1 , Land—Extension of Water Limits—Levy and Alteration of Bates and Charges—Borrowing of Money—Amend- ment, Repeal, and Incorporation of Acts). 'NOTICE IS HEREBY GIYEN. that Application is intended to be made to Parliament in the ensuing Session by the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the town of Saint Helens, in the County of Lancaster (hereinafter called the Corporation), for leave to bring in a Bill for all or some of the following purposes (that is to say) : To empower the Corporation to make and maintain the works hereinafter described, or some of them, that is to say- 1. The Kirkby Pumping Station.—A shaft or well (to be sunk to an uncertain depth) with pumps, engines, and appliances connected therewith, wholly situate in the township of Kirkby, in the parish of Walton-on-the- Hill, in and near the south-east corner of a field, which adjoins, on the fa,uth side thereof, Old Rough Cottage, stack yard, and croft, which lie and abut on the northerly side of Old Rough-lane, and which field belongs, or is reputed to belong, to the Earl of Sefton, and is in the occupation of Thomas Owen. 2. An Aqueduct or Line of Pipes, commencing in the said township and parish, at the said intended shaft or well, and terunnating in the township of Knowsley, in the parish of Huyton, by a junction with the aque- duct hereinafter described in Moss-lane, at a point fourteen chains or thereabout* south of the junction of Eicarisbrick-brow with Old Molly's-lane. which aque- duct will be a holly situate in the townships of Kirkby and Knowsley, and parishes of Walton-on-the.lllll and Huyton. 3. The Knowsley Pumping Station.—A shaft or well (to be sunk to an uncertain depth) with pumps, engines, and appliances connected therewith, wholly situate in the township of Knowsley, in the parish of Huyton, in the north-eastel ly portion of a field abutting on the north- west on the brook which forms the bJundary of the townships of Kirkby and Knowsley, and abutting as to part of such field, and on the easterly side thereof on Moss-lane, and on the ,north-easterly side thereof on the garden belonging, or attached to a. house o: cottage in Moss-lane, in the occupation of one Thomas Ratcliffe, and which field belongs, or is reputed to belong, to the Earl of Derby, and is in the occupation of Joseph Hewitt. 4. An Aqueduct or Line bf Pipes, commencing in the said township of Knowsley and parish of Huyton, at the last-mentioned intended shaft or well, and terminating In the township of Eccleston, in the parish of Preseot, in Holt-lane, at its junction with ficholes-lane, and by a junction with the existing aqueduct of the Corpora- tion, which intended aqueduct will be wholly situate in the townships of Knowsley and Eccleston, and parishes of Huyton and Prescot. All which intended works will be wholly situate in the County of Lancaster. Together with all proper and necessary wells. shafts, tun- nels, drifts, adits, pipes, valves, syphons, hydrants, junctions, tanks, basins, engines, pumps, buildings, embankments roads, and other works connected with the shafts or wells, aqueducts and works aforesaid, and which may be necessary or proper for taking, pumping, impounding, using, and distributing the waters intended to be taken. To empower the Corporation for the purposes of the intended works and Act, to purchase or acquire by compulsion or agree- ment, or to take on lease, any lands houses, or buildings, or to appropriate any lands, houses, or buildings belonging to them in the townships, parishes, and county aforesaid, and any rights, or easements in, over, or connected with any lands, houses, or buildings in the townships, parishes, and county aforesaid, and on the sale of lands to reserve water and other rights. To empower the Corporation to take, pump, divert, impound, appropriate, and use for the purposes of their water under- taking, or other the purposes of the intended Act, all springs, streams, and waters which may be found in, upon, or under any lands acquired or held by the Corporation under the powers of the intended Act, or which can, or may be taken, or intercepted by the intended works or some of them. To empower the Corporation to deviate in the construction of the intended works laterally and vertically to the extent to be shown on the plans and sections to be deposited as herein- after mentioned or to be defined in the intended Act. To authorise the Corporation to lay down, maintain, alter, and renew mains, pipes, culverts, sewers, and drains in, through, a long, under, across, and over any public highways, streets, roads, streams, paths, tramsvays and railways, and for the purposes of the intended Act to break up, cross, alter, divert, stop up (either temporarily or permanently), and inter- fere with roads, streets, highways, courts, alleys, footpaths, bridges, tramways, railways, sewers, drains, streams, brooks, water-courses, mains, pipes, and telezraphs within the parishes, townships, and places aforesaid. To extend the limits of the Corporation for supplying water to all places within the said townships of Kirkby and Knowsley. To empower the Corporation for all or any of the purposes of the intended Act to demand, recover, and levy rates, rents, and charaes for and in respect of the supply of water, to in- crease or vary existing rates, rents, and charges, and confer ex- emptions therefrom, and to apply any money belonging to, or under the control of the Corporation to all or any of the objects and purposes of the intended Act, and to borrow money for the purposes of the intended Act, and to mot tgage or charge the rates, rents, tolls, or charges levied or leviable by them, and their Gas and Water undertakings, lands and property, or some of them, as security therefor, w;th power to issue debentures, debenture stock, and annuity certificates, charge- able upon the securities in at resaid, or any of them, and to make provision for the repayment of money to be so borrowed. To vary or extinguish all existing rights and privileges, which would or might in any way prevent or interfere with or delay the accomplishment of any of the objects of the intended Act, and to confer other rights and privileges. To repeal or amend all or some of the provisions of the follow- ing Local Act, and pubic Acts of a local character, namely: The St. Beleos Improvement Act, 1869. The Local Govern- ment Board's Provisional Orders Confirmation (Helper Union, etc.) Act. 1877. The Local Government Board's Provisional Orders Confirmation (Abingdon, etc.) Act, 1878. The Local Government Board's Provisional Orders Confirmation (Aber- gavenny Union, etc ) Act, 1879, and all other Acts relating to the Corporation. The Liverpool Corporation Waterworks Act, 1847. The Liverpool Corporation Waterworks Act, 1880, and all Acts relating to the Waterworks undertaking of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Citizens of the City of Liverpool. To incorporate with or without alterations and amendments all or some of the prtivisions of the following Public Acts, namely: The Commissioners' Clauses Act, 1847. Cie Lands Clauses Consolidation Act., 1845, 1860, and 1869. The Water- works' Clauses Acts, 1847 and 1863. The Local Loans Act, 1875, and the Provisions of the Railways' Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845, with respect to the temporary ocmpation of lands and all Acts amending the same respectively or any of them, and all or some of the Provisions or the St. Helens Improvement Act, 1869. - On or before the 30th day of November instant, uplicate plans, and sections, and books of reference to such plans, to- gether with a copy of this notice as published in the London Gazette, will be deposited for public inspection with the Clerk of the Peace for the County of Lancaster, at his office at Preston, and on or before the same day a copy of so much of the said p`ans, sections, and books of reference as relates to the several parishes in or through which the said intended works are pro- posed to be made, together with a copy of this notice, will on or before the said 30th (lay of November be deposited with the Clerk of each such parish at his residence. , Printed copies of the intended Act or Bill, will, on or before the 21st day of December next, be deposited in the Pi ivate Bill Office of the House of Commons. THOMAS BREWIS, Dated this Fourth day of November. 1881. Town Clerk, Bt. Helens.
